lessons.title: FUNDAMENTALS OF AUDITING AN INTRODUCTION

shortQuestions.question: Define an audit according to ISA 200.

answerBlocks.text: Audit is an independent examination of financial statements of an entity that enables an auditor to express an opinion whether the financial statements are prepared (in all material respects) in accordance with an identified and acceptable financial reporting framework (e.g. international or local accounting standards and national legislations).

shortQuestions.question: List the essential features of an audit.

items: An auditor involves in examination of financial statements, the auditor is not responsible for the preparation of the financial statements.
The end result of an audit is an opinion to assist the user of the financial statements, relying heavily on professional judgment.
The auditor’s opinion refers to "true and fair" or "fair presentations", which is a matter of judgment.
The auditor should be independent of the entity to provide an objective, professional view.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain why there is a need for an audit.

answerBlocks.text: The need for an audit arises because owners may not believe the manager's reports due to possible errors, fraud, misleading information, or failure to disclose relevant information or conform to regulations.
An independent auditor is appointed to examine the financial statements and report on findings to solve the problem of credibility.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the problems that financial reports may have which necessitate an audit.

items: Contain errors
Not disclose fraud
Be inadvertently misleading
Be deliberately misleading
Fail to disclose relevant information
Fail to conform to regulations

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between auditing and accounting.

rows: Process of recording, classifying, summarizing and reporting financial information.
Independent examination of financial statements to express an opinion on their true and fair presentation.
Responsibility of directors to prepare financial statements using consistent accounting policies.
Auditors assess whether financial statements properly reflect financial information.
Focuses on preparing financial information for decision making.
Focuses on verifying the accuracy and fairness of financial statements.
Requires understanding of accounting principles and rules.
Requires deep knowledge of accounting and auditing standards.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the meaning of 'true and fair' in the context of an audit opinion.

answerBlocks.text: "True and fair" means that the financial statements are prepared and presented in accordance with applicable International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and local pronouncements/legislations, reflecting a fair presentation of the entity's financial position. It is a matter of professional judgment rather than a precise definition.

shortQuestions.question: Who can be appointed as an auditor for a public company or certain private companies according to the lesson?

items: The person must be a Chartered Accountant within the meaning of the Chartered Accountants Ordinance, 1961.
For listed companies, the auditor must have a satisfactory Quality Control Review (QCR) rating issued by ICAP.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the importance of auditor independence.

answerBlocks.text: Auditor independence means the auditor has no significant personal interest in the entity, allowing an objective and professional view to be taken. This independence is essential for users of the auditor’s report to have confidence in relying on the auditor’s opinion.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the challenges involved in auditing financial statements of large multinational companies.

answerBlocks.text: Large multinational companies have complex accounts involving subsidiaries with differing conventions, legal systems, accounting and control systems. The audit requires independent experts trained in assessing such financial information to ensure accuracy and compliance.

shortQuestions.question: List the types of entities other than limited companies that may require audits as mentioned in the lesson.

items: Charities
Building Societies
Financial Services businesses

lessons.title: Fundamentals of Auditing Auditing – An Introduction

shortQuestions.question: What is an auditor’s report?

answerBlocks.text: An auditor’s report is a document produced at the end of an audit in which the auditor expresses his opinion about the truth and fairness of the financial statements of an entity, addressed to the owners or stakeholders.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the primary aim of an audit.

answerBlocks.text: The primary aim of an audit is to enable the auditor to say whether the accounts show a true and fair view or do not show a true and fair view.

shortQuestions.question: List the main components included in the standard auditor’s report as per the Companies Ordinance 1984.

items: Audit of balance sheet, profit and loss account, cash flow statement, and statement of changes in equity
Statement of obtaining all necessary information and explanations
Responsibility of management for internal control and preparation of financial statements
Auditor’s responsibility to express an opinion based on audit
Opinion on proper books of accounts and conformity with Companies Ordinance
Opinion on conformity with approved accounting standards and true and fair view
Opinion on deduction and deposit of Zakat under Zakat and Usher Ordinance

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the auditor’s responsibility according to the International Auditing Standards.

answerBlocks.text: The auditor’s responsibility is to express an opinion on the financial statements based on an audit conducted in accordance with International Standards on Auditing, which includes planning and performing the audit to obtain reasonable assurance that the financial statements are free from material misstatement.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the management’s responsibility and the auditor’s responsibility in the audit process.

answerBlocks.text: **Management’s responsibility** includes preparing and fairly presenting the financial statements in accordance with applicable standards, designing and maintaining internal control, selecting accounting policies, and making reasonable accounting estimates.

**Auditor’s responsibility** is to express an opinion on the financial statements based on an audit conducted in accordance with auditing standards, including obtaining audit evidence and evaluating accounting policies and estimates.

shortQuestions.question: What does the auditor’s opinion stand for?

answerBlocks.text: The auditor’s opinion means that, in the auditor’s judgment, the financial statements show a true and fair view. The auditor does not say the statements do show a true and fair view as a fact, but expresses an opinion based on his audit.
Reliance on the auditor’s opinion depends on the auditor’s independence, honesty, and competence.

shortQuestions.question: List the three types of audits discussed in the lesson.

items: Financial statement audits
Operational audits
Compliance audits

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain what a financial statement audit is.

answerBlocks.text: A financial statement audit is conducted to determine whether the overall financial statements are stated in accordance with specified criteria, such as International Financial Reporting Standards and the Companies Ordinance 1984.
It involves verifying quantifiable information in financial statements like the balance sheet, income statement, statement of changes in equity, cash flow statement, and notes.

shortQuestions.question: What is the purpose of an operational audit?

answerBlocks.text: An operational audit reviews any part of an entity’s operating procedures and methods to evaluate efficiency and effectiveness, often resulting in recommendations for improvement.

shortQuestions.question: Give two examples of areas that may be evaluated in an operational audit.

items: Efficiency and accuracy of processing payroll transactions in a newly installed computer system
Efficiency, accuracy, and customer satisfaction in processing the distribution of letters and parcels by a courier company

shortQuestions.question: Explain the purpose of a compliance audit.

answerBlocks.text: The purpose of a compliance audit is to determine whether the entity is following specific procedures, rules, or regulations set by a higher authority.

shortQuestions.question: Who is the primary group concerned with the results of compliance audits and why?

answerBlocks.text: Management is the primary group concerned with compliance audit results because they focus on the extent of compliance with prescribed procedures and regulations within the entity.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the key parts of the definition of auditing applied to each type of audit as summarized in the lesson.

rows: Documents, records, and outside sources of evidence
Annual audit of General Motors’ payroll processing for subsidiary
Number of payroll records processed, costs, errors
Standards for efficiency and effectiveness in payroll department
Error reports, payroll records, payroll processing costs
Determine if bank loan requirements have been met
Financial statements and calculations by the auditor

shortQuestions.question: List the advantages of having financial statements audited even where no statutory requirement exists.

items: Disputes between management may be more easily settled, for example in partnerships with complicated profit sharing arrangements.
Major changes in ownership may be facilitated if past accounts contain an independent audit report.
Application to lenders or financial institutions for finance may be strengthened by submission of audited accounts.
The audit may enable the auditor to give constructive advice to management on improving business efficiency.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the disadvantages of an audit.

items: The audit fee must be paid, which discourages many partnerships and sole traders from having their accounts audited.
The audit involves the client’s staff and management in providing information, which can cause disruption.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the typical stages of an external audit.

items: Audit appointment and engagement letter.
Initial planning including knowledge of the business, risk assessment, and control procedures review.
Internal control review and accounting system review.
Preparation of the audit plan and application of analytical review techniques.
Considering ways to seek audit evidence and performing substantive testing.
Review of the financial statements for compliance and material misstatement.
Preparation and signing of the audit report.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between reliance approach and extensive substantive approach in audit evidence gathering.

answerBlocks.text: If controls are operating effectively, the auditor can reduce substantive testing and adopt a reliance approach. If controls appear weak, the auditor will not rely on them and will carry out extensive substantive testing of transactions and balances.

shortQuestions.question: What are the main responsibilities of the Executive Director/Secretary of ICAP?

items: Personnel management
Financial management
Office administration
Publications
Information systems
Conducting and performing secretarial functions for the Council and Executive Committee meetings

shortQuestions.question: List the key members assisting the Executive Director in ICAP.

items: Secretary

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the relationship between auditing firms and the term Chartered Accountants.

answerBlocks.text: Auditing firms describe themselves as Chartered Accountants. They are composed of accountants who perform audits and also provide other services beyond auditing.

shortQuestions.question: List other services commonly provided by chartered accountant firms besides auditing.

items: Writing up books of accounts (Book keeping)
Balancing books of accounts (Extracting trial balance)
Preparing final accounts
Tax management
Statutory form filling
Financial consultancy
Management and system consultancy

Investigations (Fraud audit)

shortQuestions.question: Why is an external audit primarily required in companies according to the lesson?

answerBlocks.text: Because of the split-up of ownership from control, an external audit is needed to provide independent assurance on the financial statements.

shortQuestions.question: What factors should professional auditors consider to minimize disruption during an audit?

answerBlocks.text: Professional auditors should plan their audit carefully to minimize the time and effort required from the client’s staff and management in providing information.

lessons.title: OBJECTIVE AND GENERAL PRINCIPLES GOVERNING AN AUDIT OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

shortQuestions.question: Define the objective of an audit of financial statements.

answerBlocks.text: The objective of an audit of financial statements is to enable an auditor to express an opinion whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with an identified financial reporting framework (e.g. International or Local Accounting Standards).
The opinion is expressed using terms such as “give a true and fair view” or “present fairly in all material respects”.

shortQuestions.question: List two things that an audit opinion does not provide assurance about.

items: Future viability of the entity
Efficiency or effectiveness of management

shortQuestions.question: Outline the key ethical characteristics emphasized by ICAP for auditors.

items: Independence: Auditor is independent of management and not under their control or influence.
Integrity: Auditor is honest and straightforward, not corrupt.
Objectivity: Auditor forms opinion based solely on obtained evidence, without subjectivity.
Professional Competence and Due Care: Auditor has necessary qualifications, skills, experience, and performs work with planning and diligence.
Confidentiality: Auditor does not disclose or misuse information obtained during audit without permission (except as required by law).
Professional Behavior: Auditor acts and appears professional, maintaining up-to-date knowledge and skills.
Technical Standards: Audit is performed following applicable international or national standards.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the role of International Standards on Auditing (ISAs).

answerBlocks.text: ISAs contain basic principles and essential procedures for auditing, along with related guidance. They are issued by the International Auditing Practices Committee (IAPC) to improve uniformity of auditing practice worldwide.
Auditors apply ISAs in the context of explanatory material to understand and perform audits effectively.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) and International Auditing Practice Statements (IAPSs).

rows: Provide practical assistance but do not have authority of standards
Contain basic principles, essential procedures, and related guidance
Provide guidance to implement standards and promote good practice
To be understood and applied in audits
To assist auditors in applying ISAs

shortQuestions.question: What is meant by professional skepticism in auditing?

answerBlocks.text: Professional skepticism is an attitude where the auditor plans and performs the audit with a questioning mind, critically assessing the validity of audit evidence and being alert to contradictory or unreliable information.
It means forming an opinion only after obtaining sufficient and appropriate evidence rather than blindly accepting management's explanations.

shortQuestions.question: Outline what is meant by the 'scope of an audit'.

answerBlocks.text: The scope of an audit refers to the audit procedures that, in the auditor’s judgment and based on ISAs, are appropriate in the circumstances to achieve the audit objective.

items: Audit evidence is obtained by applying necessary audit procedures.
Procedures are based on ISAs, professional bodies, legislation, regulations, and terms of engagement.

shortQuestions.question: List the management assertions for which an auditor obtains audit evidence.

items: Existence
Rights and obligations
Occurrence
Completeness
Valuation
Measurement
Presentation and disclosure

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the assertion of 'completeness' in auditing.

answerBlocks.text: Completeness asserts that there are no unrecorded assets, liabilities, transactions, events, or undisclosed items in the financial statements.
This assertion is especially important for liabilities.

shortQuestions.question: What is reasonable assurance in auditing and how is it achieved?

answerBlocks.text: Reasonable assurance is a conclusion that the financial statements are not materially misstated.
It is achieved by obtaining sufficient and appropriate audit evidence through audit procedures.

shortQuestions.question: List three inherent limitations of an audit that affect reasonable assurance.

items: Use of testing (application of procedures on samples)
Inherent limitations of accounting and internal control systems
Persuasive nature of audit evidence rather than conclusive

shortQuestions.question: Who is responsible for preparing the financial statements and who is responsible for expressing an opinion on them?

answerBlocks.text: Management is responsible for preparing and presenting the financial statements.
The auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion on the financial statements.

lessons.title: Reasonable assurance through audit evidence

shortQuestions.question: Define reasonable assurance in auditing.

answerBlocks.text: Reasonable assurance means a conclusion that the financial statements are not materially misstated. It acknowledges that an auditor cannot obtain absolute assurance due to inherent limitations.

shortQuestions.question: List the types of audit evidence mentioned in the lesson.

items: For internal control
For transactions and account balances
For financial statements

shortQuestions.question: Outline the inherent limitations of an audit that affect reasonable assurance.

items: The use of testing (application of procedures on samples).
The inherent limitations of accounting and internal control system.
The persuasive nature of audit evidence rather than conclusive.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the difference between persuasive and conclusive audit evidence.

answerBlocks.text: **Persuasive** audit evidence leads to an opinion and causes the auditor to believe the information, whereas **conclusive** audit evidence is final and convincing.

shortQuestions.question: List the inherent limitations of accounting and internal control systems as described in the lesson.

items: Management overrides
Collusion with employees
Collusion with third parties
Unaffordable cost of internal control
Human error

shortQuestions.question: Explain why an audit does not guarantee that financial statements are free from material misstatement.

answerBlocks.text: Because of inherent limitations such as sampling, limitations in accounting and internal controls, and the persuasive nature of audit evidence, absolute assurance is not attainable. Therefore, an audit cannot guarantee that financial statements are free from material misstatement.

shortQuestions.question: Define audit risk.

answerBlocks.text: Audit risk is the risk that the auditor expresses an inappropriate audit opinion when the financial statements are materially misstated.

shortQuestions.question: List the levels at which the risk of material misstatement can occur.

items: Overall financial statement level
Transactions, account balances, and disclosures level

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the auditor's responsibility regarding audit risk.

answerBlocks.text: The auditor should plan and perform the audit to reduce audit risk to an acceptably low level consistent with the objective of an audit.

shortQuestions.question: Outline management's responsibilities related to financial statements as described in the lesson.

items: Designing, implementing and maintaining internal control relevant to the preparation and presentation of financial statements free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.
Selecting and applying appropriate accounting policies.
Making accounting estimates.

lessons.title: Appointment, Duties, Rights and Liabilities of Auditor

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the audit requirement for companies regarding financial statements.

answerBlocks.text: Not all limited companies are required to have their financial statements audited. Small companies are generally exempt from the audit requirement. Small and medium sized companies may file abbreviated accounts or prepare accounts with reduced disclosures.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the procedure for the appointment of the first auditors of a company.

items: The directors shall appoint the first auditors within 60 days of incorporation.
The first auditors hold office until the first annual general meeting (AGM).
If directors fail to appoint, members shall appoint the first auditors.
If no appointment is made within 120 days, the Securities & Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) will appoint the auditors.

shortQuestions.question: List the appointing authorities and terms of office for first, subsequent, and casual vacancy auditors.

rows: SECP if not appointed at AGM
SECP if not filled within 30 days

shortQuestions.question: Explain the powers of the Securities & Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) regarding auditor appointments.

items: SECP may appoint an auditor if first auditors are not appointed within 120 days of incorporation.
SECP may appoint an auditor if subsequent auditors are not appointed at the AGM.
SECP may appoint an auditor if a casual vacancy is not filled within 30 days.
SECP may appoint an auditor if appointed auditors are unwilling to act.

answerBlocks.text: To exercise this power, the company must notify SECP within one week of the power becoming exercisable.

shortQuestions.question: Who fixes the remuneration of auditors and how does it depend on the appointing authority?

items: If auditors are appointed by directors, directors fix the remuneration.
If auditors are appointed by SECP, SECP fixes the remuneration.
In all other cases, members (the company) fix the remuneration.

answerBlocks.text: Minimum hourly rates are recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Pakistan (ICAP).

shortQuestions.question: Outline the procedure for the change or removal of subsequent auditors as per Section 253.

items: A member must give notice of the resolution to appoint another auditor at least 14 days before the AGM.
The company sends a copy of the notice to the retiring auditor and members at least 7 days before the AGM.
In listed companies, notice must be published in an English and Urdu daily newspaper.
The retiring auditor can make representations which are sent to members or read at the AGM.
The company must notify the Registrar within 14 days after the AGM about the appointment or removal of auditors.

shortQuestions.question: What are the key points regarding communication between new and previous auditors before appointment?

answerBlocks.text: Under the Chartered Accountant Ordinance, 1961, a new auditor accepting appointment without communicating with the previous auditor is guilty of professional misconduct.
The new auditor must communicate with the previous auditor to ascertain any professional objections before accepting the appointment.
The incoming auditor must ensure compliance with the Companies Ordinance, 1984 regarding appointment requirements.

shortQuestions.question: List the qualifications required for appointment as an auditor under Section 254(1).

items: Must be a Chartered Accountant within the meaning of the Chartered Accountants Ordinance, 1961.
For listed companies, must have a satisfactory Quality Control Review (QCR) rating issued by ICAP.
Applicable to public companies, private companies that are subsidiaries of public companies, and private companies with paid-up capital of three million rupees or more.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the disqualifications for appointment as an auditor listed under Section 254(3).

items: Present or past three years directors, officers, or employees of the company.
Partners or employees of directors, officers, or employees of the company.
Spouse of a director.
Persons indebted to the company.
Body corporate.
Persons or their spouses/minor children holding shares of the audit client or associated companies (must disclose and disinvest within 90 days if held prior to appointment).

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the removal procedure of auditors appointed at an annual general meeting.

items: Auditors appointed at an AGM may be removed before the next AGM by a special resolution.
A new auditor nominated by a member shall be appointed in place of the outgoing auditor.
Notice of nomination must be given to members at least 14 days before the general meeting.
SECP may appoint auditors if removal occurs.

shortQuestions.question: What actions must a company take after the AGM regarding auditor appointments or removals?

items: Notify the Registrar within 14 days after the AGM about the appointment of new auditors with their consent letter.
Notify the Registrar about the retirement or removal of auditors.

shortQuestions.question: Summarize the checklist for changing auditors including timing and required notifications.

items: Member must give notice at least 14 days before the AGM.
Company sends copy of notice to retiring auditor and members at least 7 days before AGM.
Publication of notice in newspapers before AGM (for listed companies).
Retiring auditor's representation sent to members or read at AGM.
Company notifies Registrar within 14 days after AGM.

lessons.title: RIGHTS, DUTIES AND LIABILITIES OF AUDITOR

shortQuestions.question: List the powers/rights of an auditor under section 255.

items: Right of access to books of account and vouchers (255(1)).
Right to receive information and explanations.
Right of access to books and papers of branch (255(2)).
Right to receive notices of general meetings and to attend those meetings (255(6)).
Right to make representation where another person is being appointed as auditor (253(3)).

shortQuestions.question: Outline the duties of an auditor under section 255(3).

items: To give a report to the members on the accounts, books of account, balance sheet and profit and loss account examined by him.
Where any matter reported upon is answered in the negative or with a qualification, the report shall include reasons for such qualification with factual position.
To include in the report of the company such matters as directed by the Federal Government.
To attend general meetings of a listed company, either himself or through an authorized person, in which the balance sheet, profit and loss account and the auditors' report are to be considered.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain additional duties of an auditor besides those under section 255(3).

items: To make report for inclusion in prospectus (Section 53 read with Part I of Schedule II).
To certify receipts and payments account in the statutory report (Section 157).
To make report on declaration of solvency in case of voluntary winding up.
To exercise reasonable care and skill in carrying out his duties and make such inquiries as considered necessary.

shortQuestions.question: What are the requirements related to the reading and inspection of the auditor’s report under section 256?

answerBlocks.text: The auditor’s report shall be read in the general meeting and shall be open to inspection by the members.

shortQuestions.question: What are the signing and dating requirements for an auditor’s report under section 257?

items: The person appointed as auditor shall sign the auditor's report or other documents required under the law.
The report should indicate the date and place.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the auditor’s liability for negligence with reference to case law.

answerBlocks.text: An auditor, being an agent of the shareholders, is required to carry out his duties with reasonable care and skill. Failure to do so makes him liable to compensate for any loss caused to a third party.

items: Arthur E. Green & Company Vs Central Advance & Discount Corporation Ltd. (1920): Auditor was guilty of negligence for accepting bad debts schedule without verification.
The London Oil Storage Co. Ltd. Vs Sear Hasluck & Co.: Auditors liable for failing to verify physical cash existence.
Irish Woolen Co. Ltd. Vs Tyson and Others: Auditors liable for overstating profits by not recording purchase invoices.
Kingston Cotton Mills Co. Ltd.: Auditors not liable when accepting stock certificate without suspicion.
Mckesson V Robbins (American case): Auditors have duty to test check physical stock.

answerBlocks.text: Conclusion: Auditors should inspect securities and test check stock wherever practicable, or state acceptance of certificates in their report.

shortQuestions.question: Define misfeasance in the context of auditor’s liabilities.

answerBlocks.text: Misfeasance means breach of duty where the auditor does something wrong in the performance of his duties resulting in financial loss to the company.
If the auditor does not perform his duties properly as laid down in section 255 of the Companies Ordinance, 1984, and the company suffers loss, he is liable for misfeasance.

shortQuestions.question: What are the criminal liabilities of an auditor under sections 260, 417, and 492 of the Companies Ordinance, 1984?

items: Section 260: Failure to comply with sections 157, 255, or 257 may result in a fine up to Rs. 100,000. Knowingly making a false report for profit or to cause loss may lead to imprisonment for one year.
Section 417: Charges of forgery against an auditor may lead to imprisonment up to 2 years or a fine up to Rs. 20,000 or both.
Section 492: Making a false statement in any report may result in imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine not exceeding Rs. 20,000.

shortQuestions.question: Who is qualified to audit cost accounts when a company is required to maintain records relating to costs of production?

answerBlocks.text: The auditor shall be a Chartered Accountant or a Cost and Management Accountant.

lessons.title: Lesson 8

shortQuestions.question: Define civil liabilities of an auditor.

answerBlocks.text: Civil liabilities arise in the situation when there is absence of reasonable care and skill that can be expected of a person in a set of circumstances. When negligence of an auditor is being evaluated, it is in terms of what other competent auditors would have done in the same situation.

shortQuestions.question: List the types of liabilities an auditor may face.

items: Civil Liabilities (arising from lawsuits / Liability for negligence)
Criminal Liabilities

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the duty of care under contract law for auditors.

answerBlocks.text: The company has a contract with the auditor and hence can sue the auditor for breach of contract if the auditor is negligent in carrying out the terms of the contract. Only the company can sue the auditor in contract as other people, such as banks, creditors and shareholders, are not in a contractual relationship with the company.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the professional conduct requirements auditors must follow when carrying out their duties.

items: Exercise reasonable care and skill.
Carry out professional work with due skill, care, diligence, and expedition.
Have proper regard for technical and professional standards expected of members.
Adapt the degree of skill and care to the particular situation and circumstances.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between breach of contract and tort action of negligence in auditing context.

answerBlocks.text: Breach of contract occurs when one or both parties fail to fulfill the requirements of a contract, such as a CA firm failing to deliver a tax return on the agreed date. Tort action of negligence arises when auditors fail to meet their obligations causing injury to another party other than the audit client, for example, a bank claiming the auditor failed to uncover material misstatements relied upon in granting a loan.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the significance of the Jeb Fasteners v Marks Bloom (1980) case regarding auditor liability.

answerBlocks.text: The case involved a plaintiff who acquired share capital based on audited accounts that were negligent and did not show a true and fair view. Although auditors owed a duty of care, they were not held liable because the plaintiff did not suffer loss, having decided to buy the shares regardless of the accounts. Thus, whether a duty of care existed was not directly relevant to the decision.

shortQuestions.question: List measures auditors can take to minimize their liabilities.

items: Not being negligent.
Following the International Standards on Auditing (ISAs).
Agreeing on the engagement letter.
Defining in the report the work undertaken.
Defining the purpose of the report.
Limiting liabilities to third parties.
Defining the scope of professional competence.

shortQuestions.question: What criminal liabilities can auditors face under sections 157, 255, and 257?

items: Charges of forgery (e.g., evidence created or documents forged).
Charges against false statements regarding opinion in the audit report.

shortQuestions.question: Who can initiate legal action against auditors under law of tort and law of contract respectively?

rows: Other users of financial statements (e.g., banks, creditors)

shortQuestions.question: What is meant by 'privity of contract' in the context of auditing?

answerBlocks.text: Privity of contract refers to the relationship established by a contract between parties, such as between a CA firm and a client, often formalized by an engagement letter that defines the services, fees, and timing. It is possible to have privity without a written agreement, but the engagement letter clarifies the contract.

lessons.title: BOOKS OF ACCOUNT & FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

shortQuestions.question: What is a voucher and what types of vouchers are mentioned?

answerBlocks.text: A voucher is a document prepared to record a transaction after approval, containing all descriptions and evidences of the transaction and authorization.

items: Receipt voucher
Payment voucher
Journal voucher
Petty cash voucher

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between books of original entry and books of secondary entry.

items: **Books of Original Entry:** Books where debit and credit are initially recorded systematically, e.g., purchase journal, sales journal, cash book.
**Books of Secondary Entry:** Ledgers where transactions are posted from original books to extract trial balance and prepare financial statements, e.g., main ledger, subsidiary ledger.

shortQuestions.question: List the main books of original entry used for recording business transactions.

items: Purchase journal
Sales journal
Purchase return journal
Sales return journal
Cash book (two/three column)
Petty cash book
General journal

items: Balance sheet

Notes to the accounts

shortQuestions.question: Explain the process of recording a transaction from approval to entry in the books of accounts.

items: Responsible manager approves the transaction.
Transaction takes place and is evidenced by a source document.
A voucher is prepared containing transaction details and approvals.
Voucher is authorized by the accounts manager.
Bookkeeper records the transaction in the books of accounts.

shortQuestions.question: Give examples of source documents used for different transactions.
What is the role of the journal in accounting, and how is a journal entry structured?

answerBlocks.text: The journal is the first book of account where all business transactions and events are recorded in chronological order. Both debit and credit effects are recorded systematically.

items: Debit account is written first in the particulars column with its amount in the debit column.
Credit account is written below the debit account, indented, with its amount in the credit column.
Narration explaining the transaction is included in parentheses.

shortQuestions.question: Why are journals subdivided and what are some examples of these subdivisions?

answerBlocks.text: Journals are subdivided to manage a large number of transactions efficiently, especially when there are many cash and credit transactions.

items: Cash book for cash transactions
Purchase journal for credit purchases
Sales journal for credit sales
Sales return journal for sales returns
Purchase return journal for purchase returns
General journal for other transactions

shortQuestions.question: Describe the purpose and contents of a sales journal.

answerBlocks.text: The sales journal records only credit sales transactions and includes details such as date, name of debtor, invoice number, post reference, and amount net of trade discount.

shortQuestions.question: What are trade discount and settlement terms on a sales invoice?

items: **Trade Discount:** A pre-agreed discount shown on the invoice but not recorded in the books of accounts as it has no financial effect.
**Settlement Terms:** Also known as prompt payment terms, e.g., 2/10, n/30 means a 2% discount if payment is made within 10 days; otherwise, full payment is due within 30 days.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the need for a purchase journal and its main contents.

answerBlocks.text: A purchase journal is maintained to record all credit purchases separately, excluding cash purchases. It contains date, name of creditor, invoice number, post reference, and amount.

shortQuestions.question: What supporting document evidences purchase returns and what is the role of a debit note?

answerBlocks.text: Purchase returns are evidenced by a credit note received from the seller, which reverses the purchase invoice effects.
A debit note is a request sent by the purchaser to the seller for issuance of a credit note, accompanying the rejected goods.

shortQuestions.question: Describe the structure and purpose of a cash book.

answerBlocks.text: A cash book is a book of original entry recording all cash transactions first. It has two sections: one for cash receipts (receipt side) and one for cash payments (payment side), each formatted with date, particulars, post reference, and amount.

shortQuestions.question: What are the supporting documents for cash receipts and cash payments?

items: Cash receipts are supported by copies of cash memos/receipts issued to payers and retained by the business.
Cash payments are supported by original copies of cash memos/receipts issued by recipients and attached with cash vouchers.

lessons.title: STATUTORY REQUIREMENTS REGARDING COMPANY ACCOUNTS

shortQuestions.question: Define the types of books of account a company is required to keep under Section 230.

items: Cash received and expended by the company.
Sales and purchases of goods by the company.
All assets and liabilities of the company.
For companies engaged in production, processing, manufacturing, or mining, a production record as required by the Commission.

shortQuestions.question: List the penalties for directors of a listed company failing to comply with the books of account provisions under Section 230.

items: Imprisonment for one year.
Fine not less than Rs. 20,000 and not more than Rs. 50,000.
Further fine of Rs. 5,000 per day during which the default continues.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the timeline for presenting the first and subsequent annual accounts under Section 233.

answerBlocks.text: The first annual accounts must be presented before the AGM within eighteen months from the date of incorporation.
Subsequent annual accounts should be presented at least once every calendar year before an AGM, within three months of the date of the balance sheet.
The Commission or registrar may extend this period by up to two months.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the requirements for sending copies of accounts and reports to members before the AGM.

answerBlocks.text: Copies of accounts, auditor’s report, and directors’ report must be sent to every member at least twenty-one days before the Annual General Meeting.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the preparation of balance sheet contents for listed companies and other companies as per Section 234.

items: Listed companies and private/non-listed public subsidiaries of listed companies prepare accounts according to the Fourth Schedule, including statements of changes in equity and cash flow statements, with IFRS adopted by SECP.
Other companies prepare accounts according to the Fifth Schedule, also including statements of changes in equity and cash flow statements, with IFRS adopted by SECP.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the treatment of surplus arising on revaluation of fixed assets under Section 235.

items: Surplus on revaluation should be transferred to 'Surplus on revaluation of fixed assets account' shown after capital and reserves in the balance sheet.
Surplus shall not be reduced except to set off decreases in revaluation or upon disposal of the revalued asset.
Depreciation on revalued assets is based on revalued amounts and charged to the Profit and Loss Account.
Incremental depreciation is transferred from the surplus account to un-appropriated profit/loss through the Statement of Changes in Equity.

shortQuestions.question: List the disclosures required in the director’s report for a public company or a private company subsidiary of a public company under Section 236.

items: Business affairs and proposed dividend, if any.
Amounts set aside to reserves, if any.
Material changes and commitments affecting financial position between year end and report date.
Material changes in the nature of business during the year.
Explanation of any qualification in auditor’s report.
Pattern of shareholding (percentage held by parties).
Name and country of incorporation of holding company if outside Pakistan.
Earnings per share.
Reasons for loss and future profit prospects, if any.
Information about defaults in payment of debts and reasons.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the requirements for consolidated financial statements of holding companies under Section 237.

answerBlocks.text: Holding companies with subsidiaries must attach consolidated financial statements presenting the group as a single enterprise, complying with Fourth Schedule and International Accounting Standards.
Subsidiaries with financial years ending more than three months before the holding company's year end must prepare interim financial statements for consolidation.
Auditors of holding companies must report on consolidated financial statements and review subsidiary interim statements.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the signing requirements for the balance sheet under Section 241.

answerBlocks.text: The balance sheet must be approved by the Board of Directors and signed by the chief executive and one director.
If the chief executive is temporarily out of Pakistan, two directors must sign and provide a statement explaining the reason.

shortQuestions.question: What are the filing requirements for copies of the balance sheet with the registrar under Section 242?

items: Listed companies must file three copies of audited accounts and auditor’s report within thirty days from the AGM.
Other companies must file two copies.
Private companies are not required to file accounts with the registrar.

shortQuestions.question: Describe the rights of members and debenture-holders regarding copies of accounts and auditor’s reports under Sections 243 and 247.

answerBlocks.text: Members and debenture-holders or their trustees have the right to obtain copies of the annual accounts and auditor’s report of the company upon payment.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the quarterly accounts requirements for listed companies under Section 245.

items: Listed companies must prepare and send profit and loss accounts and balance sheets within one month after each quarter to members and stock exchanges.
Three copies must be filed with the registrar and the Commission.
Quarterly accounts for the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd quarters must be circulated within one month of quarter end.
Board of directors’ approval is mandatory for circulation.
Non-compliance results in fines on directors including chief executive and chief accountant.

shortQuestions.question: What authority does the SECP have under Section 246 regarding additional statements of accounts and reports?

answerBlocks.text: The SECP may require companies or classes of companies to prepare and send periodical statements of accounts, information, or other reports to members, registrar, SECP, stock exchange, or others in specified form, manner, and time.
For listed companies and subsidiaries, SECP directed providing other information in annual reports to external auditors for review of material inconsistencies since 1st January 2006.

lessons.title: Lesson 11

shortQuestions.question: Define the auditor's requirement regarding understanding the entity and its environment.

answerBlocks.text: The auditor should obtain an understanding of the entity and its environment, including its internal control, sufficient to identify and assess the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements whether due to fraud or error, and sufficient to design and perform other audit procedures.

shortQuestions.question: List the main areas of guidance provided by the standard for understanding the entity and its environment.

items: Risk assessment procedures and sources of information about the entity and its environment including its internal control.
Understanding the entity and its environment, including its internal control.
Assessing the risk of material misstatement.
Communicating with those charged with governance and management.
Documentation.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the risk assessment procedures an auditor should perform to understand the entity and its environment.

items: Inquiries of management and others within the entity.
Analytical procedures.
Observation and inspection.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the role of inquiries in risk assessment procedures.

answerBlocks.text: Inquiries involve obtaining information from management and those responsible for financial reporting, as well as others within the entity such as production staff, internal audit personnel, and other employees. These inquiries help the auditor understand the environment, internal control effectiveness, accounting policies, legal matters, marketing strategies, and other relevant aspects.

shortQuestions.question: List examples of persons within the entity from whom the auditor may make inquiries.

items: Those charged with governance (e.g., board representatives, chief finance officers).
Internal audit personnel.
Employees involved in initiating, processing, or recording complex or unusual transactions.
In-house legal counsel (e.g., company secretary, legal advisor).
Marketing or sales personnel.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the types of information obtained from inquiries directed towards internal audit personnel and marketing personnel.

rows: Activities concerning monitoring and effectiveness of internal control.
Changes in the entity’s marketing strategies.
Whether management has responded satisfactorily to audit findings.
Sales trends or contractual arrangements with customers.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the purpose of analytical procedures in the risk assessment process.

answerBlocks.text: Analytical procedures include ratio analysis, trend analysis, and common size analysis of financial and non-financial information. They enable the auditor to identify situations where significant fluctuations exist, expected relationships are not present, or unexpected relationships occur.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the types of observation and inspection procedures used in understanding the entity and its environment.

items: Observation of entity activities and operations.
Inspection of documents such as business plans, strategies, records, and internal control manuals.
Reading reports prepared by management and those charged with governance.
Visits to the entity’s premises and plant facilities.
Tracing transactions through the information system relevant to financial reporting (walk-through).

shortQuestions.question: Explain the purpose of discussions among the audit team during risk assessment.

answerBlocks.text: Discussions among the engagement team members help to share knowledge and exchange information about the susceptibility of the entity’s financial statements to material misstatements, fostering a better understanding and assessment of risks.

lessons.title: Understanding the Entity and Its Environment, including Its Internal Control

shortQuestions.question: List the main aspects included in the auditor’s understanding of the entity and its environment.

items: Industry, regulatory, and other external factors, including the applicable financial reporting framework
Nature of the entity, including the entity’s selection and application of accounting policies
Objectives and strategies and the related business risks that may result in a material misstatement of the financial statements
Measurement and review of the entity’s financial performance
Internal control

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the importance of understanding industry conditions for an auditor.

answerBlocks.text: Understanding industry conditions helps the auditor to assess factors such as market and competition, cyclical or seasonal activity, product technology, and energy supply and cost, which may affect the entity’s financial statements.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the types of regulatory environment factors an auditor should consider.

items: Accounting principles and industry-specific practices
Regulatory framework for regulated industries
Legislation and regulations significantly affecting the entity’s operations
Regulatory requirements like labor laws and minimum wage rate
Direct supervisory activities (e.g., NAB, Excise & Taxation Department)
Taxation including corporate and other taxes
Government policies affecting the entity’s business such as monetary, fiscal, financial incentives, tariffs, and trade restrictions
Environmental requirements affecting the industry and entity

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the nature of the entity and its industry environment.

answerBlocks.text: The nature of the entity refers to its operations, ownership, governance, investments, structure, and financing, while the industry environment includes external factors like market competition, regulatory framework, and economic conditions affecting the entity.

shortQuestions.question: List examples of business operations aspects an auditor should understand about the entity.

items: Nature of business (e.g., manufacturer, wholesaler, banking)
Products or services and markets, including major customers and contracts
Conduct of operations such as production stages and business segments
Alliances, joint ventures, and outsourcing activities
Geographic dispersion and industry segmentation
Location of production facilities, warehouses, and offices
Key customers
Involvement in electronic commerce
Important supplies of goods and services
Employment details including wage levels and union contracts
Research and development activities and expenditures
Transactions with related parties

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain what is meant by the entity’s financial reporting understanding.

answerBlocks.text: It involves understanding the accounting principles and industry-specific practices, revenue recognition, accounting for fair values, foreign currency transactions, industry-specific categories, accounting for unusual or complex transactions, and financial statement presentation and disclosure.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the types of investments an auditor should consider when understanding the entity.

items: Acquisitions, mergers, or disposals of business activities
Capital investment activities including plant and equipment
Investments and dispositions of securities and loans
Investments in non-consolidated entities such as partnerships and joint ventures
Group structure including major subsidiaries and associated entities
Debt structure including covenants, restrictions, guarantees, and off-balance-sheet financing
Leasing of property, plant, or equipment
Beneficial owners and related parties
Use of derivative financial instruments

shortQuestions.question: List examples of other external factors currently affecting the entity’s business that an auditor should consider.

items: General level of economic activity such as recession or growth
Interest rates and availability of financing
Inflation
Currency revaluation

shortQuestions.question: Explain why an auditor should assess the appropriateness and consistency of accounting policies selected by the entity.

answerBlocks.text: Assessing appropriateness and consistency ensures that the accounting policies comply with the financial reporting framework and industry practice, and that they are applied consistently to provide reliable financial statements.

lessons.title: Understanding the Entity and Its Environment, Including Its Internal Control

shortQuestions.question: List the sources through which an auditor obtains an understanding of the entity and its environment, including its internal control.

items: Risk assessment procedures and sources of information about the entity and its environment including its internal control.
Understanding the entity and its environment, including its internal control.
Assessing the risk of material misstatement.
Communicating with those charged with governance and management.
Documentation.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the types of risk assessment procedures used by auditors to obtain an understanding of the entity.

items: Inquiries directed towards those charged with governance, middle management, legal counsel, marketing or sales personnel, and internal audit personnel.
Analytical procedures including financial and non-financial analysis.
Observation and inspection such as observing activities and operations, inspecting documents and records, reading management reports, and visiting premises and plant facilities.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the aspects of the entity and its environment that an auditor must understand.

items: External factors including industry conditions, regulatory environment, and macroeconomic level factors.
Nature of the entity including business operations, financing, financial reporting, and investments.
Objectives and strategies and the related business risks.
Measurement and review of the entity’s financial performance.
Internal control.

shortQuestions.question: Define business risk and give examples of related matters an auditor may consider.

answerBlocks.text: Business risk is the risk that objectives and strategies would not be met.

items: Industry developments (e.g., lack of expertise to deal with technological changes).
New products and services (e.g., increased product liability).
Expansion of the business (e.g., inaccurate demand estimation).
New accounting requirements (e.g., incomplete or improper implementation).
Regulatory requirements (e.g., increased legal exposure).
Current and prospective financing requirements (e.g., loss of financing).
Use of IT (e.g., incompatible systems and processes).

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between business risk and risk of material misstatement.

answerBlocks.text: Business risk is broader than the risk of material misstatement. Business risks may not cause any misstatement in the financial statements but can affect the going concern of the entity.

shortQuestions.question: List conditions and events that may indicate risks of material misstatement.

items: Operations in economically unstable regions.
Operations exposed to volatile markets.
High degree of complex regulation.
Going concern and liquidity issues.
Constraints on availability of capital and credit.
Changes in the industry or supply chain.
Developing or offering new products or services.
Expanding into new locations.
Large acquisitions or reorganizations.
Entities or segments likely to be sold.
Complex alliances and joint ventures.
Use of off-balance-sheet finance and complex financing arrangements.
Significant transactions with related parties.
Lack of personnel with appropriate accounting skills.
Changes in key personnel.
Weaknesses in internal control.
Inconsistencies between IT strategy and business strategies.
Changes in IT environment.
Past misstatements or significant adjustments.
Significant non-routine transactions.
Transactions recorded based on management’s intent.
Application of new accounting pronouncements.
Accounting measurements involving complex processes.
Events involving significant measurement uncertainty.
Pending litigation and contingent liabilities.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain how an auditor uses inquiries as a risk assessment procedure.

answerBlocks.text: The auditor directs inquiries towards those charged with governance, middle management, legal counsel, marketing or sales personnel, and internal audit personnel to obtain relevant information about the entity and its environment including internal control.

shortQuestions.question: What are the potential related business risks when implementing a strategy?

answerBlocks.text: Potential related business risks when implementing a strategy include effects leading to new accounting requirements such as incomplete or improper implementation.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the auditor’s understanding of the nature of the entity.

items: Business operations.
Financing.
Financial reporting.
Investments.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the importance of understanding the entity’s objectives and strategies in auditing.

answerBlocks.text: Understanding the entity’s objectives and strategies helps the auditor identify related business risks that may result in material misstatement of the financial statements.

lessons.title: Objectives and strategies and the related business risks

shortQuestions.question: Define internal control as per the lesson text.

answerBlocks.text: Internal controls is the process designed and effected by those charged with governance, management, and other personnel to provide reasonable assurance about the achievement of the entity’s objectives with regard to reliability of financial reporting, effectiveness and efficiency of operations and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

shortQuestions.question: List the components of internal control mentioned in the lesson.

items: The control environment
The entity’s risk assessment process
The information system, including the related business processes relevant to financial reporting and communication
Control activities
Monitoring of controls

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain why understanding internal control is important for an auditor.

answerBlocks.text: Understanding of Internal Control is used by the auditor to identify types of potential misstatements and to consider factors that affect the risks of material misstatements and design the nature, timing and extent of further audit procedures.

shortQuestions.question: Outline examples of matters an auditor may consider to understand the measurement and review of the entity’s financial performance.

items: Key ratios and operating statistics
Key performance indicators
Employee performance measures and incentive compensation policies
Trends
Use of forecasts, budgets and variance analysis
Analyst reports and credit rating reports
Competitor analysis
Period-on-period financial performance (revenue growth, profitability, leverage)

shortQuestions.question: What types of information may create pressures on the entity and motivate management to misstate the financial statements?

answerBlocks.text: Performance measures, internal and external, sometimes create pressures on the entity and motivate management to misstate the financial statements.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between internal and external information sources useful for understanding the entity’s financial performance.

answerBlocks.text: Internally generated information may highlight the entity’s position vis-à-vis its competitors, while reports from credit rating agencies and analysts provide external information useful to the auditor’s understanding of the entity and its environment.

shortQuestions.question: List the risk assessment procedures mentioned in the lesson text.

items: Inquiries
Analytical procedures
Observation & Inspection
Risk assessment procedures
External Factors

shortQuestions.question: Explain how internal control is related to business risks according to the lesson.

answerBlocks.text: Internal control is designed and implemented to address identified business risks that threaten the achievement of the entity’s objectives regarding financial reporting reliability, operational effectiveness and efficiency, and compliance with laws and regulations.

shortQuestions.question: What role does communication play in the context of understanding the entity and assessing risks?

answerBlocks.text: Communication is part of the process to obtain understanding of the entity and its environment and to assess the risks of material misstatement, though the lesson text does not elaborate further.

shortQuestions.question: Why is documentation important in the audit risk assessment process?

answerBlocks.text: Documentation is important to record the auditor’s understanding of the entity and its environment and the assessed risks of material misstatement, supporting the audit strategy and procedures.

lessons.title: The Entity’s Risk Assessment Process

shortQuestions.question: Define internal control as described in the lesson.

answerBlocks.text: Internal control is the process designed and affected by those charged with governance, management, and other personnel to provide reasonable assurance about the achievement of the entity’s objectives with regard to reliability of financial reporting, effectiveness and efficiency of operations, and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

shortQuestions.question: List the five components of internal control mentioned in the lesson.

items: The control environment
The entity’s risk assessment process
The information system, including related business processes relevant to financial reporting and communication
Control activities
Monitoring of controls

shortQuestions.question: Outline the elements encompassed by the control environment.

items: Communication and enforcement of integrity and ethical values
Commitment to competence
Participation by those charged with governance
Management’s philosophy and operating style
Organizational structure
Human resource policies and practices

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the entity’s risk assessment process.

answerBlocks.text: The entity’s risk assessment process is the process of identifying and responding to business risks that affect the entity’s financial reporting. It includes how management identifies risks affecting the ability to produce financial statements that give a true and fair view, estimates their significance and likelihood, and decides upon actions to manage them.

shortQuestions.question: List examples of circumstances that may give rise to risks relevant to financial reporting.

items: Changes in operating environment
New personnel
New or revamped information systems
Rapid growth
New technology
New business models, products or activities
Corporate restructurings
Expanded foreign operations
New accounting pronouncements

shortQuestions.question: What are the main components of the information system relevant to financial reporting?

items: Infrastructure (physical and hardware components)
Software
People
Procedures
Data

shortQuestions.question: Describe the purposes of an information system in financial reporting as given in the lesson.

items: Describe transactions timely and in sufficient detail for proper classification
Identify and record all valid transactions
Measure the value of transactions to permit proper monetary recording
Determine the time period of transactions for proper accounting period recording
Present properly the transactions and related disclosures in the financial statements

shortQuestions.question: Explain the role of communication in internal control.

answerBlocks.text: Communication involves providing an understanding of individual roles and responsibilities pertaining to internal control, understanding roles of others, and doing exception reporting to higher level management. It may take forms such as policy manuals, accounting and financial reporting manuals, memoranda, and can be made electronically, orally, or through management actions.

shortQuestions.question: List the types of control activities included in internal control.

items: Performance reviews
Information processing
Physical controls
Segregation of duties

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the purpose of segregation of duties as a control activity.

answerBlocks.text: Segregation of duties involves assigning different people the responsibilities of authorizing transactions, recording transactions, and maintaining custody of assets to reduce opportunities for any person to both commit and conceal errors or fraud in the normal course of their duties.

shortQuestions.question: What does monitoring of controls include according to the lesson?

items: Ensuring internal controls operate as intended
Assessing the quality of internal control performance over time
Ongoing activities or separate evaluations or a combination
Supervision functions of managers
Internal audit
Communication from external parties indicating areas requiring attention

shortQuestions.question: Outline the auditor’s responsibilities in assessing the risk of material misstatement.

items: Identify risks throughout understanding the entity and its environment, including relevant controls
Relate identified risks to what can go wrong at the assertion level
Consider whether risks could result in material misstatement of financial statements
Consider likelihood that risks could result in material misstatement

shortQuestions.question: What are significant risks and why do they require special audit considerations?

answerBlocks.text: Significant risks relate to non-routine transactions, such as those involving judgmental matters, greater management or manual intervention, or complex calculations or accounting principles. They require special audit considerations because they may have a higher risk of material misstatement.

shortQuestions.question: When should the auditor revise the risk assessment during an audit?

answerBlocks.text: The auditor should revise the risk assessment and modify further planned audit procedures when tests of controls or substantive procedures reveal that controls are not performing effectively and misstatements found are not in accordance with expectations.

lessons.title: (b) Adequate documents and record.

shortQuestions.question: Define the term 'Control environment' as used in internal control structure.

answerBlocks.text: **Control environment** refers to the overall attitude, awareness, and actions of management regarding the internal control system, including management's philosophy and the functioning of the audit committee.

shortQuestions.question: List three elements or factors that affect the control environment.

items: Management's philosophy
Functioning of the audit committee
Segregation of duties

shortQuestions.question: Outline the objectives of internal controls related to accounting systems.

items: Identify and record all valid transactions
Permit proper classification of transactions
Preparation of reliable financial reports

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the role of 'adequate documents and records' in internal control.

answerBlocks.text: Adequate documents and records ensure that all transactions are properly supported and recorded, providing a basis for verification and audit. An example includes pre-numbered receiving reports.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between 'independent check on performance' and 'control procedures' in the context of internal controls.

answerBlocks.text: **Independent check on performance** refers to activities such as reconciliations and audits that verify the accuracy of records and operations, whereas **control procedures** are the policies and actions like segregation of duties designed to prevent or detect errors and irregularities.

shortQuestions.question: Fill in the blank: Members can appoint the auditors if they are not appointed by the Directors within ____ days of incorporation.

answerBlocks.text: 60 days

lessons.title: DOCUMENTING THE INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEM

shortQuestions.question: List the principal benefits of a sound system of internal control to an entity.

items: Assurance that all transactions are completely and accurately processed.
Confidence that only authorized transactions take place.
Assurance that adequate documentation supporting transactions is created and retained.
Assurance that the company’s assets and liabilities are correctly stated for informed decision-making.
Minimization of the risk of fraud and misappropriation of assets.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain how a sound system of internal control benefits the auditor.

answerBlocks.text: A good system of internal control helps promote a situation where the financial statements present a true and fair view, making the auditor's work easier.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the auditor’s responsibilities regarding internal control according to international standards on auditing.

items: Obtain an understanding of the accounting and internal control system sufficient to plan the audit and develop an effective audit approach.
Use professional judgment to assess the components of audit risk and design audit procedures to reduce risk to an acceptably low level.

shortQuestions.question: What is the mnemonic used to summarize the categories of internal control? List all categories represented by it.

answerBlocks.text: The mnemonic is SOAP MAPS.

items: Supervision
Organization
Arithmetic and Accounting
Physical
Management and Monitoring
Authorization
Personnel
Segregation of duties

shortQuestions.question: Define the category 'Supervision' in internal control and give a possible application.

answerBlocks.text: Supervision means there should be adequate supervision of work to ensure that controls are being complied with.
Possible application: a supervisor or manager reviews and checks the work of a subordinate.

shortQuestions.question: What does the 'Organization' category of internal control require? Provide an example.

answerBlocks.text: Enterprises should have a formal, documented organization structure with clear lines of responsibility.
Example: lines of authority within an organization make it clear which individuals are responsible for decisions and transactions.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the importance of 'Arithmetic and Accounting' controls with an example.

answerBlocks.text: The company should ensure adequate controls to guarantee completeness and accuracy of its financial records.
Example: use of control accounts, reconciliation procedures, and arithmetic checks on accounting records.

shortQuestions.question: What is meant by 'Physical' controls in internal control? Give an example.

answerBlocks.text: Physical controls ensure the security and safekeeping of assets such as plant, machinery, inventory, and cash.
Example: banking cash immediately, controlling access to inventory areas, electronic tagging of inventory.

shortQuestions.question: Describe the 'Authorization' control category with an example.

answerBlocks.text: All transactions should be authorized.
Example: authorization of purchases, cash and bank payments, sales on credit, bad debt write-offs.

shortQuestions.question: What is the purpose of 'Segregation of duties' and how is it applied in practice?

answerBlocks.text: Segregation of duties involves dividing responsibilities to reduce opportunities for fraud and manipulation by ensuring no one person controls a transaction from start to finish.
Example: in inventory purchasing, different persons handle initiation, authorization, custody, and recording.

shortQuestions.question: List the methods auditors use to document the internal control system.

items: Organization chart
Narrative notes
Flowcharts
Internal control questionnaires (ICQs)
Internal control evaluation checklists (ICEC)

shortQuestions.question: What are the advantages of using flowcharts to document accounting systems?

items: They portray the flow of documents through the system and relate movements with procedures and checks.
They show sources and destinations of all documents clearly.
They help highlight weaknesses in business controls.
They enable audit tests to be clearly related to weaknesses in the accounting system.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the essentials that internal control evaluation flowcharts must highlight.

items: The sequence of operations happening to each document (e.g., authorization, checking, matching, filing).
The segregation of staff duties and who is responsible for each operation.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly describe the narrative notes method for documenting systems and mention two shortcomings.

answerBlocks.text: Narrative notes involve drawing up a written description of the system for audit files, describing processes and responsibilities.

items: Notes can take up a disproportionate amount of space.
Notes may be difficult to interpret and may become outdated if personnel change.

lessons.title: EVALUATING THE INTERNAL CONTROL SYSTEM

shortQuestions.question: Define the Document symbol in flow charts and explain how movement of documents is represented.

answerBlocks.text: The Document symbol represents each document in the flowchart and is associated with a vertical flow-line. Vertical flow-lines represent movement in time within a particular department. When a document moves to another department, this movement is shown by a horizontal line. Departments are listed across the page, and only vertical and horizontal lines are used, never diagonal lines.

shortQuestions.question: List the main operations represented by the Operation symbol in a flow chart.

items: Preparation of a document
Adding up totals
Using the document to prepare other documents
Any operation other than a check function

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the use of the Information flow symbol in flow charts.

answerBlocks.text: The Information flow symbol is used when one document is prepared from another. The movement of information is shown by a dotted horizontal line, which always runs horizontally and never vertically. The flow-lines continue for both the original and the new document.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the purpose of the Check symbol in flow charts and give examples of its use.

answerBlocks.text: The Check symbol represents verification or checking functions in the flowchart. It can show a simple check on a single document, such as totaling an invoice, or a check between two documents, for example, verifying that all goods dispatched have been invoiced.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between temporary and permanent filing symbols in flow charts.

answerBlocks.text: Both temporary and permanent files use the same filing symbol, but temporary files are marked with the letter 'T'. Temporary filing symbols must have the flow-line continue, indicating the document is still in process. Permanent filing symbols cause the flow-line to stop, indicating the document has reached its ultimate destination.

shortQuestions.question: What is the significance of the book of account symbol in flow charts?

answerBlocks.text: The book of account symbol shows books which already exist and also depicts the re-filing of the book once posting is completed. The flow-line principles for books are the same as for documents, with a vertical flow-line ending with the re-filing of the book, which is kept chronologically.

shortQuestions.question: Explain how multi-part sets of documents are depicted in flow charts.

answerBlocks.text: Each part of a multi-part set of documents must have a flow-line emanating from it. For example, in a purchase order set, one part may be sent to the supplier, another to a department, and another filed numerically. Each part is shown separately with its own flow-line.

shortQuestions.question: What are the auditor's options after preliminary evaluation of the internal control system?

items: Rely on internal controls and adopt a systems audit approach
Perform extensive substantive testing using a verification approach

shortQuestions.question: List the main features of an Internal Control Questionnaire (ICQ).

items: Used in large company audits
Used to place reliance on internal controls
Used to design audit approach

shortQuestions.question: Outline the objectives of an Internal Control Questionnaire (ICQ).

items: To ascertain a client's systems of accounting and internal control
To evaluate the control system thus recorded

shortQuestions.question: Describe the construction and design considerations of an Internal Control Questionnaire (ICQ).

answerBlocks.text: When designing ICQs, it is good practice to include a brief introduction listing control objectives for each sub-system and any business considerations specific to the enterprise. Questions should ascertain whether control objectives are achieved and cover authorization, documents, recording, sequence, custody, segregation of duties, and instructions to staff. Questions are framed for Yes/No answers, where No indicates a control weakness. The ICQ should include basic information such as the document name, system, client, accounting period, preparer and reviewer, and columns for Yes/No answers, comments, audit program references, and Management Letter references.
