shortQuestions.question: Define an Internal Control Questionnaire (ICQ).

answerBlocks.text: An ICQ is a formal and usually standardized document which comprises a list of internal controls in existence and highlights any weaknesses.

shortQuestions.question: List the main objectives of an Internal Control Questionnaire.

items: To ascertain a client's systems of accounting and internal control.
To evaluate the control system thus recorded.
To identify controls indicating strengths in the system for auditor reliance.
To identify weak or no control areas requiring extensive substantive testing and reporting in the Management Letter.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the features of an Internal Control Questionnaire.

items: Used in large company audits.
Used to place reliance on internal controls.
Used to design audit approach.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the construction considerations for an ICQ.

items: State a brief introduction including a list of control objectives each sub-system should achieve.
Include any business considerations specific to the enterprise.
Design questions to ascertain whether control objectives are achieved covering instructions, authorization, documents, recording, custody, and segregation of duties.
Frame questions for Yes/No answers where No indicates a control weakness.
Include basic information such as document name, related system, client, accounting period, preparer and reviewer evidence, and columns for answers, comments, and references.

shortQuestions.question: What are the control objectives of the purchasing cycle as described in the ICQ example?

items: Purchased goods/services are ordered under proper authorities and procedures.
Goods/services are ordered only as necessary and from suitable suppliers.
Goods/services received are inspected for quality, quantity, and condition.
Invoices and related documentation are properly checked and approved before being recorded as trade payables.
All transactions related to trade payables are valid and accurately recorded.

shortQuestions.question: List some business considerations affecting the audit procedures in the purchasing cycle.

items: Nature of the company’s purchases.
Existence of a purchasing department.
The company’s purchasing policy including inventory levels and supplier management.

shortQuestions.question: What information should an ICQ carry according to the lesson?

items: Name of the document (ICQ).
The system to which it relates (e.g., purchasing cycle).
The client to whom it relates.
The accounting period under review.
Evidence of who has prepared and reviewed the document.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the main criticism of Internal Control Questionnaires (ICQs).

answerBlocks.text: ICQs can become too complex, lengthy, and detailed for meaningful evaluation of accounting systems. They may provoke a too formalized approach focusing on controls themselves rather than on the fraud or irregularity the controls are designed to prevent.

shortQuestions.question: What is an Internal Control Evaluation Checklist (ICEC) and how does it differ from an ICQ?

answerBlocks.text: An ICEC is a document designed to determine whether desirable internal controls are present by using key control questions to ascertain where specific frauds or errors are possible. It is normally used when system information has already been recorded, usually in flowcharts.
Unlike ICQs, ICECs are shorter and less complex but may require more skill and judgment to interpret. They use key questions that prompt supplementary questions and refer to supporting flowcharts.

shortQuestions.question: List some inherent limitations of internal control systems as mentioned in the lesson.

items: The need to balance the cost of control with its benefits.
Controls apply mainly to regular transactions, not unusual or one-off transactions.
Potential for human error.
Possibility of fraudulent collusion to circumvent controls.
Abuse of authority and override of controls by senior management or owners.
Obsolescence of controls due to changes in business activities or organization.

shortQuestions.question: Why is it important for auditors not to rely entirely on internal controls?

answerBlocks.text: Because all internal control systems have inherent limitations and may not prevent errors or fraud completely, auditors always carry out some verification of transactions as part of their work, regardless of how effective the controls appear.

shortQuestions.question: What are some key aspects that ICQ questions should cover to ascertain if control objectives are achieved?

items: Instructions given to staff in performing their duties.
Authorization procedures.
Documents and procedures used to originate transactions.
Recording procedures.
Sequence of procedures.
Custody procedures.
Relative independence of persons involved at each stage (segregation of duties).

shortQuestions.question: Define audit evidence and list the main types of audit procedures used to obtain it.

answerBlocks.text: Audit evidence is the information obtained by the auditor through audit procedures that allows a conclusion to be reached.

items: Test of control (compliance test)
Test of details (substantive test)
Analytical procedures (substantive test)

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain how the auditor’s understanding of internal control affects audit procedures.

answerBlocks.text: The auditor’s understanding of the control environment determines the nature, timing, and extent of audit procedures.

items: A strong control environment allows more confidence in internal controls and may permit some procedures at interim dates.
Weaknesses in controls require more procedures at period end, more substantive evidence, or expanded audit scope.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the three audit approaches based on the understanding of internal control.

items: Apply tests of control only for a particular assertion.
Apply substantive procedures only for a particular assertion if no effective controls are identified.
Combined approach: applying both tests of controls and substantive procedures for the same assertion.

answerBlocks.text: In very small entities with no control activities, only substantive procedures may be applied.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the nature, timing, and extent of audit procedures.

rows: Purpose of the procedure (tests of controls or substantive) and type (inspection, observation, inquiry, confirmation, recalculation, re-performance, analytical procedures).
When audit procedures are performed or the period/date to which the evidence applies.
Sample size or number of observations; quantity of audit evidence obtained.

shortQuestions.question: List factors the auditor considers when deciding the timing of audit procedures.

items: The control environment.
When relevant information is available (e.g., electronic files).
The nature of the risk (e.g., risk of inflated revenues).
The period or date to which the audit evidence relates.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the three aspects tested in tests of control.

items: Design: Whether controls are properly designed to cover the intended risk (examined through ICQs and ICECs).
Implementation: Whether controls have been put into operation (examined through walk-through tests).
Operating effectiveness: Whether controls operated effectively during the period (examined through compliance tests).

shortQuestions.question: Briefly describe the nature of tests of controls.

items: Inquiry and observation (e.g., observing controls over cash receipts).
Re-performance (e.g., preparing bank reconciliations).
Inspection of documentation relevant to controls.
Applying computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs).

shortQuestions.question: When may tests of controls be performed and what is the significance of timing?

answerBlocks.text: Tests of controls may be performed at a particular time or over the entire audit period.

items: At a particular time, evidence relates only to that time (e.g., inventory count observation).
Over the entire period, evidence covers operating effectiveness throughout the audit period.

shortQuestions.question: List the factors an auditor considers in determining the extent of tests of controls.

items: Frequency of control performance during the period.
Length of time auditor relies on the control.
Relevance and reliability of audit evidence supporting control effectiveness.
Degree of planned reliance on the control.
Expected deviation rate from the control.

shortQuestions.question: Define substantive procedures and explain their purpose.

answerBlocks.text: Substantive procedures are audit procedures performed to detect material misstatements at the assertion level.

items: Include tests of details of transactions, account balances, disclosures.
Include substantive analytical procedures.
Designed responsive to assessed risk of material misstatement.

shortQuestions.question: What audit procedures should be included in the auditor’s substantive procedures related to the financial statement closing process?

items: Agreeing the financial statements to the underlying accounting records.
Examining material journal entries and other adjustments made during preparation of financial statements.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the considerations for timing when performing substantive procedures at an interim date.

items: Control environment and relevant controls.
Availability of necessary information at a later date.
Objective of the substantive procedure.
Assessed risk of material misstatement.
Nature of the class of transactions or account balance and related assertions.
Ability to perform additional procedures to cover remaining period.

answerBlocks.text: Further substantive or combined procedures should be performed to cover the period from interim date to period end.

shortQuestions.question: List factors influencing the extent of substantive procedures performed by the auditor.

items: Risk of material misstatement due to weaknesses in internal control.
Use of audit sampling or other selective testing methods.
Possibility of testing entire population where appropriate.

shortQuestions.question: What audit procedures should the auditor perform to evaluate the adequacy of presentation and disclosure in financial statements?

answerBlocks.text: The auditor should perform audit procedures to evaluate whether the overall presentation and related disclosures comply with the applicable financial reporting framework.

shortQuestions.question: Define substantive procedures in auditing.

answerBlocks.text: Substantive procedures are performed in order to detect material misstatements at the assertion level, such as occurrence, completeness, accuracy, valuation, existence, rights and control. They include tests of details of classes of transactions, account balances and disclosures, and substantive analytical procedures.

shortQuestions.question: List the three things tested in tests of controls.

items: Design – that the internal controls are properly designed to cover the risk it is meant for.
Implementation – that the internal controls have been implemented.
Operating effectiveness – that the systems of internal control were operating effectively at relevant times during the period.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain how the design of internal control is tested.

answerBlocks.text: The proper design of internal control is tested through Internal Control Questionnaires (ICQs) and Internal Control Evaluation Checklists (ICEC).

shortQuestions.question: Outline the types of substantive procedures used in auditing.

items: Test of details – examples include testing land, debtors, and building rent.
Analytical procedures – such as comparing payroll with previous month’s salary or production cost with number of units produced.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between substantive analytical procedures and tests of details.

answerBlocks.text: Substantive analytical procedures are applied on large volumes of transactions that are predictable over time, while tests of details are more appropriate to obtain audit evidence regarding certain assertions about account balances, including existence and valuation.

shortQuestions.question: List factors an auditor considers in designing substantive analytical procedures.

items: Suitability of using analytical procedures given the assertions.
Reliability of the data including source, comparability, nature, and controls over preparation.
Whether the expectation is sufficiently precise to identify material misstatement.
Accuracy of expected results prediction.
Degree of information disaggregation.
Availability of financial and non-financial information.
Acceptable amount of difference from expected values considering materiality and possibility of misstatement.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the timing considerations for substantive procedures.

answerBlocks.text: Year-end substantive procedures are always more reliable. When substantive procedures are performed at an interim date, the auditor should perform further substantive procedures or combine them with tests of controls to cover the remaining period to provide a reasonable basis for extending audit conclusions to the period end.

items: Control environment and relevant controls.
Availability of information at a later date.
Objective of the substantive procedure.
Assessed risk of material misstatement.
Nature and frequency of transactions or account balances.
Auditor’s ability to perform procedures covering remaining period.

shortQuestions.question: What should an auditor do if misstatements are detected at an interim date?

answerBlocks.text: If misstatements are detected in classes of transactions or account balances at an interim date, the auditor ordinarily modifies the related assessment of risk and the planned nature, timing, or extent of substantive procedures covering the remaining period.

shortQuestions.question: List the assertions about classes of transactions and events for the period under audit.

items: Occurrence – transactions and events recorded have occurred and pertain to the entity.
Completeness – all transactions and events that should have been recorded have been recorded.

shortQuestions.question: Describe the assertions about account balances at the period end.

items: Existence – assets, liabilities, and equity interests exist.

Valuation and allocation – assets, liabilities, and equity interests are included at appropriate amounts and valuation or allocation adjustments are properly recorded.

shortQuestions.question: What are the assertions about presentation and disclosure in financial statements?

items: Occurrence and rights and obligations – disclosed events, transactions and other matters have occurred and pertain to the entity.
Completeness – all disclosures that should have been included have been included.
Classification and understandability – financial information is appropriately presented and described, and disclosures are clearly expressed.
Accuracy and valuation – financial and other information are disclosed fairly and at appropriate amounts.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the types of audit procedures for obtaining audit evidence.

items: Inspection of records or documents – examining internal or external records in paper or electronic form.
Inspection of tangible assets – physical examination of assets to provide evidence of existence.
Inquiry – seeking information from knowledgeable persons inside or outside the entity, formal or informal.
Confirmations – obtaining representations directly from a third party such as debtors, creditors, bankers, or legal advisors.

answerBlocks.text: Audit evidence is all the information used by the auditor in arriving at the conclusions on which his opinion is based and includes the information contained in the accounting records underlying the financial statements and other information.

shortQuestions.question: List the sources from which an auditor may obtain audit evidence.

items: Accounting records of the entity (internal source)
Other information such as minutes of meetings, confirmations from third parties, analysis reports, benchmarking data, controls manuals
Information obtained by audit procedures like inquiry, observation, inspection
Information from previous audits and firm’s quality control procedures
External sources such as suppliers, customers, bankers, legal advisers

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the terms 'sufficiency' and 'appropriateness' of audit evidence.

answerBlocks.text: **Sufficiency** is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence. **Appropriateness** is the measure of quality, i.e., relevance and reliability in providing support for detecting misstatements in account balances, classes of transactions, disclosures, and relevant assertions.

shortQuestions.question: Outline factors that affect the quantity of audit evidence needed.

items: Risk of misstatement: the greater the risk, the more audit evidence is likely to be required
Quality of audit evidence: the higher the quality, the less quantity may be required

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between internal and external sources of audit evidence.

answerBlocks.text: Internal sources include the accounting system, management, employees, and underlying documentation within the entity. External sources include third parties such as suppliers, customers, bankers, legal advisers, and other parties who have knowledge of the enterprise.

shortQuestions.question: List generalizations useful in assessing the reliability of audit evidence.

items: Audit evidence obtained from independent sources outside the entity is more reliable.
Evidence generated internally is more reliable when related controls are effective.
Evidence obtained directly by the auditor is more reliable than that obtained indirectly or by inference.
Written evidence is more reliable than oral representation.
Audit evidence provided by original documents is more reliable than that provided by photocopies and facsimiles.

shortQuestions.question: Explain why consistency of audit evidence from different sources is important.

answerBlocks.text: Auditor’s reliance increases when audit evidence obtained from one source is consistent with that from another source. If evidence is inconsistent, further procedures may be performed to resolve the discrepancies.

Payment should be made to the correct employees.
Liabilities to the tax authorities for tax and social security should be properly recorded.

shortQuestions.question: List the control objectives related to payroll deductions in a wages and salaries system.

items: Payroll and payroll deductions (tax and social security) should be calculated accurately.
Liabilities to the tax authorities for tax and social security should be properly recorded.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the importance of making payments only to authorized employees in a wages and salaries system.

answerBlocks.text: Making payments only to authorized employees ensures that wages and salaries are not fraudulently paid to unauthorized or fictitious persons, thereby safeguarding the client's resources.

shortQuestions.question: Outline how wages and salaries payments should be made in accordance with records of work performed.

answerBlocks.text: Payments should be based on accurate records of work performed such as time worked, output produced, or commissions on sales, to ensure that employees are paid correctly for their actual work.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between payment at authorized rates of pay and payment to the correct employees as control objectives.

answerBlocks.text: Payment at authorized rates of pay ensures that employees receive wages or salaries according to approved pay scales or agreements, while payment to the correct employees ensures that the payments are made to the actual individuals entitled to receive them.

shortQuestions.question: List the control objectives that ensure accuracy in the calculation and recording of payroll deductions.

items: Payroll and payroll deductions (tax and social security) should be calculated accurately.
Liabilities to the tax authorities for tax and social security should be properly recorded.

lessons.title: CONTROL PROCEDURES - WAGES AND SALARIES (a) Approval and control of documents

shortQuestions.question: List the control objectives in respect of a wages and salaries system.

items: Payment of wages and salaries should be made only in respect of the client's authorized employees.
Payment should be made at authorized rates of pay.
Wages and salaries payments should be in accordance with records of work performed, e.g. time, output, commissions on sales.
Payroll and payroll deductions (tax and social security) should be calculated accurately.
Payment should be made to the correct employees.
Liabilities to the tax authorities for tax and social security should be properly recorded.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the authorization controls recommended for the payroll system.

items: Written authorization to employ or dismiss any employee.
Changes in rates of pay authorized in writing by an official outside the wages department.
Overtime worked authorized in advance by a manager or supervisor.
An independent official reviews and signs the payroll.
Wages cheque signed by two signatories and agreed with the signed payroll.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the importance of clock cards in the payroll system.

answerBlocks.text: Clock cards should be used where weekly pay relates to hours at work to record attendance and hours worked.
There should be supervision of the cards and timing devices, especially when employees are clocking-on or off, to ensure accuracy and prevent fraud.

shortQuestions.question: What controls are suggested to ensure the quality of work in a piece work payment system?

answerBlocks.text: Payment should only be made for work of an appropriate quality which has been inspected and approved.

shortQuestions.question: List the key points related to arithmetical accuracy in payroll preparation.

items: Payroll should be prepared from clock cards, job cards, etc., and a sample checked for accuracy against current rates of pay.
Payroll details should be checked for accurate calculation of deductions such as tax, social security, pensions, and trade union subscriptions.

shortQuestions.question: Describe the role of control accounts in the payroll system.

items: Control accounts should be maintained for each deduction showing amounts paid periodically to authorities like Inland Revenue and trade unions.
Overall analytical checks should be carried out to highlight major discrepancies, such as checking against budgets and personnel records.
Management should exercise overall review and control over these accounts.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the recommended procedures when wages are paid in cash.

items: Employees should sign for their wages.
No employee should be allowed to take the wages of another employee.
Late claims for wages require the employee to sign for the wage packet and the release must be authorized.
The system should allow employees to check wages before opening packets, using specially designed wage packets.
The wages department should be separate from receipts or payments functions.
Duties of wages staff should be rotated to prevent any employee from handling all functions for a department.
The employee making up pay packets should not be the one preparing the payroll.
Surprise attendance at pay-out should be made periodically by an independent official.
Unclaimed wages should be recorded in a register and held by someone outside the wages department until claimed or re-banked after a predefined period.
An official should investigate reasons for unclaimed wages promptly.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the suggested tests of controls for wages and salaries.

items: Test sample of time sheets, clock cards or other records for approval by responsible official, with attention to overtime approval.
Test authority for payment of casual labor, especially if paid in cash.
Observe wages distribution for adherence to procedures including employee signatures and re-banking of unclaimed wages.
Test authorization for payroll amendments by reference to personnel records.
Test control over payroll amendments.
Examine evidence of checking payroll calculations, e.g. signature of financial controller.
Examine evidence of approval of payrolls by responsible official.
Examine evidence of independent checks of payrolls, e.g. internal audit.
Examine explanations for payroll expense variances.
Test authorities for payroll deductions.
Test controls over unclaimed wages.
Inspect payroll reconciliations.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the roles of the wages supervisor and the independent official in the payroll system.

answerBlocks.text: A wages supervisor may perform some of the authorization duties such as approving employment or pay changes.
An independent official reviews and signs the payroll and may conduct surprise attendance at pay-out to ensure compliance with procedures.

lessons.title: Lesson 28

shortQuestions.question: Define the central control objectives in testing the cash system.

items: All sums due to the company are received and subsequently accounted for.
No payments are made which should not be made.
All receipts and payments are promptly and accurately recorded.

shortQuestions.question: List the main control procedures over cash receipts and payments mentioned in the lesson.

items: Controls over cash receipts by post
Controls over cash collected by salesmen and representatives
Controls over cash sales
Controls over banking of receipts
Controls over cheque payments
Bank reconciliations
Controls over petty cash

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain why businesses are advised to conduct cash transactions by cheque or bank transfers.

answerBlocks.text: Controls over cheque transactions are easier to establish and maintain than controls over cash in the form of notes and coins.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the controls over cash receipts by post.

items: Use a locked mailbox and restrict access to keys to safeguard against interception.
Supervise the opening of post by a responsible official; have at least two persons present if mail volume is significant.
Restrictively cross all cheques and postal orders 'Account payee only, not negotiable' immediately upon opening.
Make an immediate record of cheques, postal orders, and cash received.
Ensure cashier and sales ledger personnel do not access receipts before recording.
Keep receipts in a locked safe and bank them immediately.
Date stamp the post to provide evidence of receipt dates and prevent 'teeming and lading'.

shortQuestions.question: List the controls over cash collected by salesmen and representatives.

items: Clearly define authority to collect cash.
Require salesmen to remit cash and report sales regularly.
Have a responsible official follow up salesmen who do not submit returns promptly.
Record collections when received, e.g., in a rough cash book or copies of receipts.
Reconcile collector's cash receipts to eventual banking promptly.
Periodically check salesmen's receipt books against cash book entries.
Independently reconcile inventory with sales and cash received if salesmen hold inventories.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish the controls over cash sales regarding recording and reconciliation.

items: Cash sales should be recorded at the point of sale using a cash till or pre-numbered cash sale invoices/receipts.
Maintain a register of cash sale books and retain copies of invoices or receipts.
Reconcile cash received daily with till roll or invoice totals.
Bank cash promptly and check daily banking against till roll or invoice totals.
Investigate any differences found in reconciliation.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the importance of independence in the reconciliation of cash sales.

answerBlocks.text: The reconciliation of cash received with till rolls or invoice totals should be carried out by someone independent of those receiving the cash and recording the sale to ensure objectivity and prevent fraud.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the procedures related to cancelled cash sale invoices.

items: A responsible official should sign cancelled cash sale invoices at the time of cancellation.
All cancelled invoices should be periodically checked for sequential numbering.

shortQuestions.question: What is 'teeming and lading' and how do controls over cash receipts by post help prevent it?

answerBlocks.text: 'Teeming and lading' is the process where cash received on one day is banked as representing different receipts on a later day. Date stamping the post provides evidence of when remittances are received and helps prevent this practice.

lessons.title: of controls as practical as possible.

shortQuestions.question: Define the control procedures over banking of receipts.

items: Receipts should be banked daily and intact, with no cash payments made from cash receipts.
Each day's receipts should be recorded promptly in the cash book.
Sales ledger personnel should have no access to cash or preparation of the paying-in slip.
Periodically compare the split of cash and cheques received and banked as recorded.

shortQuestions.question: List the key controls over cheque payments.

items: Unused cheques should be held securely.
Cheque preparer should not handle purchase or sales ledger.
Cheques signed only with evidence of approved transactions.
Supporting documents signed and cancelled as paid.
Approvers independent from cheque signatories in large concerns.
Restrict cheque signatories to minimum practical number.
Require at least two signatories except for small amounts.
Prohibit signing blank cheques or cheques payable to signatory.
Cross cheques 'A/c Payee only' if not pre-printed.
Dispatch cheques immediately or keep in safe place.
Returned cheques checked against records.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the importance of bank reconciliations and the controls associated with them.

answerBlocks.text: Bank reconciliations should be prepared regularly, at least monthly, to ensure accuracy of cash records.

items: Preparation should be independent of receipts and payments functions or independently checked.
Independent preparer should obtain bank statements directly and hold them until reconciliation is complete.
Reconciliation should include checking samples of receipts and payments against bank statement items.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the controls over petty cash management.

items: Formal level and location of cash floats established.
Restricted access to cash floats and secure holding (e.g., locked drawer or safe).
All expenditure requires a voucher signed by a responsible official, not the petty cashier.
Use of imprest system to reimburse the float.
Vouchers produced before cheque to top up cash float is signed and cancelled after reimbursement.
Minimum amount set for petty cash payments to discourage bypassing normal procedures.
Petty cash book maintained with prompt entries.
Periodic reconciliation of petty cash float by an independent person.
Rules to prevent IOUs or cashing of cheques for employees.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the responsibilities of personnel involved in cheque preparation and cheque signing.

items: Person preparing cheques should not have responsibility over purchase or sales ledger to prevent conflicts.
Cheque signatories should only sign cheques when proper approved transaction evidence is available.
In large concerns, those approving original documents should be independent from cheque signatories.
Cheque signatories should be limited in number and prohibited from signing blank cheques or cheques payable to themselves.

shortQuestions.question: List the tests of control related to cash receipts.

items: Attend mail opening to ensure procedures are followed.
Test independent check of cash receipts to bank lodgments.
Test for sequence check on pre-numbered cash receipts.
Test authorization of cash receipts.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the procedures to test controls over cash payments.

items: Test for arithmetical checks on cash received records.
Inspect cheque books for sequential use, controlled custody of unused cheques, and absence of signatures on blank cheques.
Ensure paid invoices are marked 'paid' to avoid double payment.
Test for arithmetical checks on cash payment records including cash book.
Examine evidence of authority for standing orders and direct debits.

shortQuestions.question: What are the key tests of control for bank reconciliations?

items: Examine evidence of regular bank reconciliations, usually monthly.
Check for independent review of bank reconciliations, such as a signature.
Verify follow-up of outstanding items, especially old un-presented cheques.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly describe the tests of control for petty cash.

items: Test petty cash vouchers for proper approval.
Test cancellation of paid petty cash vouchers.
Test for arithmetical checks on petty cash records.
Examine evidence of independent check of petty cash balance.

lessons.title: Control Procedures over Inventory (i) Approval and Control of Documents

shortQuestions.question: Define the general purpose of other systems the auditor may encounter in a business.

answerBlocks.text: Other systems the auditor may encounter are generally concerned with the safe custody of an asset of the business.

shortQuestions.question: List the control objectives related to inventory records.

items: Authorization and purchase procedures
Control over goods inwards inventory records supported by physical inventory counts
Control over dispatches and goods outwards
Adequate steps to identify inventory requiring provisions due to net realizable value below cost
Inventory levels controlled to ensure availability without unnecessary excess
Reviews of damaged, obsolete and slow moving inventory with authorized write-offs
Issues from inventories only on properly authorized requisitions

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the importance of arithmetical accuracy in inventory control.

items: All receipts and issues should be recorded on inventory cards cross-referenced to GRN or requisition documents.
Costing department should allocate direct and overhead costs to work-in-progress according to completion stage.
Standard costs are normally used and must be regularly reviewed to reflect actual costs.
Periodic checks of actual units against work-in-progress records should be performed.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the role of control accounts in inventory management.

answerBlocks.text: Total inventory records may be maintained and integrated with the main accounting system.
They should be reconciled to detailed inventory records and any discrepancies investigated.

shortQuestions.question: List the procedures for comparing physical inventory to records.

items: Inventory levels should be periodically checked against records by an independent person.
Material differences should be investigated.
Where perpetual records are inadequate, a full inventory count should be held at least once a year.
Maximum and minimum inventory levels should be predetermined and regularly reviewed.
Re-order quantities should be predetermined and regularly reviewed.

shortQuestions.question: Describe the control measures related to the physical storage of inventory.

items: Separate centers should be identified for holding goods.
Deliveries from suppliers should pass through a goods inwards section to stores.
All goods should be recorded and checked as received in stores.
Inventories should be held safely to prevent damage or theft.
All inventory lines should be identified and held together in marked bins with relevant information.
Access to stores should be restricted.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain tests of controls over inventory.

items: Observe physical security and environment of inventories.
Test procedures for recording inventory movements in and out.
Test authorization for adjustments to inventory records.
Test authorization for write-offs or scrapping of inventories.
Test controls over recording inventory movements belonging to third parties.
Test authorization procedures for inventory movements using goods received and dispatch notes.
Inspect reconciliations of inventory counts to records.
Check sequences of dispatch and goods received notes for completeness.
Assess adequacy of inventory counting procedures and attend counts.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the control procedures for goods inwards and goods outwards in inventory management.

answerBlocks.text: Control over goods inwards involves recording and checking deliveries from suppliers through a goods inwards section to stores.
Control over goods outwards involves ensuring dispatches are properly authorized and recorded to maintain accurate inventory records.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the importance of authorization in inventory issues and write-offs.

answerBlocks.text: Issues from inventories should be made only on properly authorized requisitions to ensure control and accountability.
Any write-offs of damaged, obsolete or slow moving inventory should be authorized to prevent unauthorized losses.

shortQuestions.question: Explain how inventory levels should be controlled according to the lesson.

items: Materials should be available when required.
Inventory should not be unnecessarily large.
Maximum and minimum inventory levels should be predetermined and regularly reviewed.
Re-order quantities should be predetermined and regularly reviewed.

lessons.title: on disposal, new technology etc.

shortQuestions.question: Define the control objectives related to non-current assets.

items: Non current assets are correctly recorded, adequately secured and properly maintained.
Acquisitions and disposals of non current assets are properly authorized.
Acquisitions and disposals of non current assets are for the most favorable price possible.
Non current assets are properly recorded, appropriately depreciated, and written down where necessary.

shortQuestions.question: List the control procedures over non current assets.

items: Annual capital expenditure budgets should be prepared by someone directly responsible to the board of directors.
Budgets should be agreed by the board and put in the minutes if acceptable.
Applications for authority to incur capital expenditure should be submitted to the board for approval with reasons, estimated cost, and any non current assets replaced.
A document showing what is to be acquired should be signed as authorized by the board or an authorized official.
Non current assets manufactured or constructed by the company should be separately identifiable in costing records reflecting direct costs plus relevant overhead but not profit.
Disposal of non current assets should be authorized and proceeds related to the authority.
A register of non current assets should be maintained for each major group identifying each item with cost and depreciation details.
Physical inspection of non current assets should be carried out periodically and checked against the asset register with discrepancies noted and investigated.
Assets should be properly maintained and adequately insured.
Depreciation rates should be authorized and a written policy produced.
Depreciation should be reviewed annually to assess the need for changes.
Calculation of depreciation should be checked for accuracy.
Non current assets should be reviewed for the need for any write-down.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the purpose of maintaining a register of non current assets.

answerBlocks.text: A register of non current assets is maintained for each major group of assets to identify each item within that group and to contain details of cost and depreciation.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the tests of controls related to non current assets.

items: Check authorization of purchase against board minutes, capital expenditure budgets, and capital expenditure form.
Check authorization for disposals of significant assets.
Confirm existence of non current asset register which adequately identifies assets and comments on their current condition, ensuring reconciliation to nominal ledger.
Test evidence of reconciliation of register to physical checks of existence and condition of assets.
Check authorization of depreciation rates and particularly any changes in rates.
Examine evidence of checking the correct calculations of depreciation.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between the systems approach and the verification approach in auditing non current assets.

answerBlocks.text: The systems approach focuses on the accounting systems and is supplemented by a reduced amount of substantive testing when controls are found effective.
The verification approach involves full substantive testing and is used when controls are not working effectively.

shortQuestions.question: Explain why depreciation rates should be authorized and reviewed annually.

answerBlocks.text: Depreciation rates should be authorized to ensure they are appropriate and consistent with company policy.
Annual review is necessary to assess the need for changes in depreciation rates in light of profits or losses.

shortQuestions.question: What control procedures should be followed for non current assets manufactured or constructed by the company itself?

answerBlocks.text: Such assets should be separately identifiable in the company's costing records and should reflect direct costs plus relevant overhead but not include any profit.
An example is a building company constructing its own office block.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the importance of physical inspection of non current assets.

answerBlocks.text: Physical inspection is carried out periodically to check the existence and condition of non current assets against the asset register.
Any discrepancies found should be noted and investigated to maintain accuracy and control.

shortQuestions.question: List the documents and approvals required for capital expenditure on non current assets.

items: Annual capital expenditure budgets prepared by responsible personnel and agreed by the board.
Applications for authority to incur capital expenditure submitted to the board containing reasons, estimated cost, and any assets replaced.
A document showing what is to be acquired signed as authorized by the board or an authorized official.

shortQuestions.question: Why should disposal of non current assets be authorized and proceeds related to the authority?

answerBlocks.text: Authorization ensures disposals are properly approved and controlled.
Relating proceeds to the authority ensures that sales are conducted for the most favorable price possible and recorded correctly.

lessons.title: (b) Assertions about account balances at the period end.

shortQuestions.question: Define the term 'verification' in the context of auditing.

answerBlocks.text: To verify means to establish the truth of something. In auditing, verification work involves gathering evidence to conclude whether classes of transactions, balances, and disclosures in the client’s financial statements are properly stated (true and fair).

shortQuestions.question: List the five audit-testing procedures available to the auditor during verification.

items: Inspection
Observation
Enquiry
Computation
Analytical procedures

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the role of substantive testing in audit verification.

answerBlocks.text: Substantive testing procedures are designed to give evidence relating to the figures in the financial statements rather than control tests. They help the auditor verify the accuracy and truthfulness of the amounts and disclosures presented.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the five assertions about classes of transactions and events for the period under audit.

items: Occurrence – transactions and events recorded have occurred and pertain to the entity.
Completeness – all transactions and events that should have been recorded have been recorded.
Accuracy – amounts and other data relating to recorded transactions and events have been recorded appropriately.
Cutoff – transactions and events have been recorded in the proper period.
Classification – transactions and events have been recorded in the proper accounts.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between 'existence' and 'rights and obligations' assertions about account balances.

answerBlocks.text: **Existence** asserts that assets, liabilities, and equity interests actually exist at the balance sheet date. **Rights and obligations** assert that the entity holds or controls the rights to assets, and liabilities are the obligations of the entity.

shortQuestions.question: List the four assertions about presentation and disclosure in financial statements.

items: Occurrence and rights and obligations – disclosed events, transactions and other matters have occurred and pertain to the entity.
Completeness – all disclosures that should have been included have been included.
Classification and understandability – financial information is appropriately presented and described, and disclosures are clearly expressed.
Accuracy and valuation – financial and other information are disclosed fairly and at appropriate amounts.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the general audit objective of verification work.

answerBlocks.text: The general objective of audit verification work is to establish whether the financial statements present a true and fair view.

shortQuestions.question: What are the primary financial statements that the auditor reviews during verification?

items: Balance sheet
Income statement
Statement of changes in equity
Cash flow statement
Notes to the accounts

shortQuestions.question: Outline the main elements of financial statements as defined in the lesson.

items: Assets: rights or other access to future economic benefits controlled by an entity as a result of past transactions or events.
Liabilities: obligations of an entity to transfer economic benefits as a result of past transactions or events.
Owners' equity: arrived at by deducting liabilities from assets.
Gains and losses: determined in terms of increases and decreases in owners' equity.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the recognition principle for assets and liabilities in financial statements.

answerBlocks.text: Assets and liabilities should be recognized when there is evidence of their existence and they can be reliably measured. They should be derecognized when the rights (assets) or obligations (liabilities) no longer exist.

shortQuestions.question: When are substantive audit procedures primarily performed and why?

answerBlocks.text: Substantive audit procedures are primarily performed at or very soon after the client's year end because they normally rely on the availability of draft financial statements and allow verification of individual assets and liabilities.

shortQuestions.question: List factors that the auditor considers when deciding whether to perform substantive procedures at an interim date.

items: The control environment and other relevant controls.
The availability of information necessary for the auditor’s procedures at a later date.
The objective of the substantive procedure.
The assessed risk of material misstatement.
The nature of the class of transactions or account balance and related assertions.
The auditor's ability to perform appropriate substantive procedures or tests of controls to cover the remaining period.

shortQuestions.question: What is the relationship between the risk of material misstatement and the extent of substantive procedures performed?

answerBlocks.text: Greater risk of material misstatement due to weaknesses in internal control systems leads to a greater extent of substantive procedures being performed by the auditor.

lessons.title: Disposals -. Vouch the authority - minutes or company procedures.

shortQuestions.question: Define vouching and verification in the context of auditing assets.

answerBlocks.text: **Vouching** is the inspection of supporting documents and records. **Verification** involves inspection, observation, enquiry, computation, and analysis to confirm the accuracy and existence of assets.

shortQuestions.question: List the aspects of assets that must be verified by an auditor.

items: Cost
Authorization
Value
Existence
Beneficial Ownership
Presentation in the accounts

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the mnemonic CAVE BOP used in asset verification.

answerBlocks.text: CAVE BOP stands for the key aspects of asset verification: Cost, Authorization, Value, Existence, Beneficial Ownership, and Presentation in the accounts.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the verification procedures for assets acquired during the year under review.

items: Vouch the cost with documentary evidence such as invoices.
Vouch the authority for acquisition with minutes or authorized delegated authority.

shortQuestions.question: What verification methods are used for depreciation, amortization, and other write downs of assets?

items: Vouch authorization of policy with minutes.
Examine adequacy and appropriateness of policy.
Check calculations.
Investigate revaluations.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between existence and ownership in asset verification.

answerBlocks.text: Existence means the asset physically exists, while ownership means the legal right to the asset. Existence does not imply ownership; for example, an asset may be present but owned by a third party.

shortQuestions.question: List the verification procedures used to confirm existence and ownership of assets.

items: Physical inspection of the asset.
Inspection of title deeds and certificates of ownership.
External verification such as letters of acknowledgement from banks or debtors.
Ancillary evidence like rate demands, repair bills, and other outgoings.
Confirmation of investment ownership by receipt of dividends and interest.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the importance of presentation and value in asset verification.

answerBlocks.text: Appropriate accounting policies must be adopted, consistently applied, and adequately disclosed. Materiality and classification of assets affect the true and fair view of financial statements. The choice of disclosure and description impacts how assets are presented.

shortQuestions.question: Outline other matters relevant to asset verification that an auditor should consider.

items: Letter of representation from management.
Being 'put upon enquiry' when something seems unreasonable or suspicious.
Assets pledged or mortgaged as security and related liabilities.
Taxation and capital allowance computations in accordance with asset accounts.
Insurance coverage matching the assets in the balance sheet.
Verification of assets held by third parties.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain how assets can be verified at dates other than the balance sheet date.

items: Verify assets at an earlier date and reconcile with acquisitions and disposals to the balance sheet date.
Verify assets at an earlier date, parcel them up and seal the parcels, then at balance sheet date examine acquisitions, vouch proceeds of disposals, and check that other items are still sealed.

lessons.title: LETTER OF REPRESENTATION VERIFICATION OF LIABILITIES

shortQuestions.question: Define letter of representation in auditing.

answerBlocks.text: A letter of representation is a letter obtained by the auditor from management, addressed to the auditor, confirming any representations given by management during the audit. It is also known as the management letter.
In this context, representations are statements made to convey an opinion.

shortQuestions.question: List reasons why auditors obtain a letter of representation.

items: Auditors need to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to determine with reasonable confidence whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement.
Representations from management serve as a source of audit evidence.
In some cases, knowledge of facts or judgments is confined to management and cannot be corroborated by other evidence.
Written confirmation helps the auditor form an opinion when corroborating evidence is unavailable.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain when management representations are particularly important as audit evidence.

answerBlocks.text: Management representations are particularly important when:

items: Knowledge of the facts is confined to management, such as management's intentions affecting asset values.
The matter is principally one of judgment or opinion, for example, the readability or valuation of old stock.
In these cases, the auditor ensures no conflicting evidence exists and obtains written confirmation of representations.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the procedures an auditor should adopt regarding uncorroborated oral representations by management.

items: Summarize all material matters subject to uncorroborated oral representations in working papers.
Ensure these matters are either formally minuted and approved by the Board of Directors at a meeting ideally attended by the auditor, or included in the signed letter of representation.

shortQuestions.question: Why should standard letters of representation not be used?

items: Each audit is different and requires tailored attention.
The letter is important and should receive very careful attention.
Management should participate in producing the letter, involving drafting, review, and discussion.

shortQuestions.question: Describe the recommended timing and approval process for the letter of representation.

answerBlocks.text: The letter of representation should be:

items: Prepared starting at an early stage, such as at the beginning of the final audit, to avoid refusal by management to sign.
Approved and minuted at a board meeting ideally attended by the auditor.
Signed at a high level, for example by the chief executive or financial director.
Approved as late as possible in the audit, after the analytical review but before the audit report is prepared.
Dated on the day the financial statements are approved.

shortQuestions.question: What steps should an auditor take if management refuses to cooperate in signing the letter of representation?

items: Persuade management to cooperate.
Prepare a statement setting out the auditor's understanding of principal representations and request management confirmation.
Discuss and negotiate with management if they disagree to reach a correct understanding.
If management refuses altogether, consider whether sufficient information has been obtained and possibly qualify the audit report on grounds of limitation of scope.

shortQuestions.question: What type of matters should be included in the letter of representation?

items: Only matters which are material to the financial statements.
Matters for which the auditor cannot obtain independent corroborative evidence.

answerBlocks.text: Routine matters such as existence of fixed assets or stock valuation at lower of cost and net realizable value should not be included.

shortQuestions.question: List the four main duties of auditors in verification of liabilities.

items: Verify the existence of liabilities shown in the balance sheet.
Verify the correctness of the monetary amount of such liabilities.
Verify the appropriateness of the description given in the accounts and the adequacy of disclosure.
Verify that all existing liabilities are actually included in the accounts.

shortQuestions.question: Outline general principles or procedures auditors should apply in verifying liabilities.

items: Request or prepare a schedule showing opening balance, changes, and closing balance for each liability.
Verify cut-off to ensure liabilities relate to the correct accounting period.
Consider the reasonableness of the liability and check for suspicious circumstances.
Determine, evaluate, and test internal control procedures, especially for trade creditors.
Check clearance of liabilities from previous accounting dates.
Verify compliance with terms and conditions of loans.
Seek authority for liabilities from company or directors' minutes and relevant documents.
Examine relevant documents such as invoices and debenture deeds.
Enquire about security for liabilities and ensure registration of charges.
Vouch the creation of each liability, e.g., receipt of loan.
Ensure appropriate accounting policies are adopted and applied consistently.
Obtain management's letter of representation.
Check interest and other ancillary evidence related to loans.
Verify proper disclosure in accordance with Companies Acts.
Perform external verification directly with creditors where possible.
Consider materiality and post-balance sheet events.
Ensure liabilities are accounted for according to accounting standards.
Assess risk of misstatement.

shortQuestions.question: Explain why it is important for auditors to ensure inclusion of all liabilities in the accounts.

answerBlocks.text: Auditors must be satisfied not only that all recorded liabilities are correct and included in the accounts, but also that no liabilities exist which are unrecorded for various reasons.

Unrecorded liabilities could materially affect the financial statements and include items such as claims by employees, unfunded pension liabilities, bonuses, tax liabilities, pending lawsuits, and others.

shortQuestions.question: List examples of unrecorded liabilities that auditors should be aware of.

items: Claims by employees for injury.
Claims by ex-employees for unfair dismissal.
Contributions to superannuation schemes.
Unfunded pension liabilities.
Liability to 'top-up' pension schemes.
Bonuses under profit sharing arrangements.
Returnable packages and containers.
Value added and other tax liabilities.
Claims under warranties and guarantees.
Liabilities on debts factored with recourse.
Bills receivable discounted.
Pending lawsuits.

shortQuestions.question: Outline actions an auditor should take to detect unrecorded liabilities.

items: Enquire of directors and other officers about possible liabilities.
Obtain a letter of representation confirming management's assertions.
Examine post balance sheet events including purchase invoices and cash book after the balance sheet date.
Review minutes of meetings where unrecorded liabilities may be mentioned.
Review current and previous years' working papers.
Maintain awareness of possibilities of unrecorded liabilities throughout the audit.

shortQuestions.question: Define equity as per the lesson.

answerBlocks.text: Equity consists of share capital and reserves and represents the interest of the owners in the net assets of the entity.

shortQuestions.question: List the aspects an auditor verifies to confirm owners' equity.

items: Share capital is properly classified and described in the accounts
Movement in share capital is properly authorized and correctly presented
Reserves are properly classified and presented
Movements in reserves are properly authorized

shortQuestions.question: Outline the verification methods used to check that share capital is properly classified and described in the accounts.

items: Check disclosure using Company Accounts Checklist
Agree authorized capital with memorandum of association
Agree issued capital with form A, or obtain certificate from registrar
Obtain list of shareholders

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain how the auditor verifies that movements in share capital are properly authorized and correctly shown.

items: Ensure shareholders’ pre-emption rights have been respected
Check that directors were authorized to allot shares
Ensure proper authorization for share redemption
Check authority for share capital reductions
Agree all movements to statement in lieu of prospectus, board minutes, memorandum and articles of association
Consider special rules for allotments of public company shares
Test allotments with supporting evidence and trace entries in register
Test payments with supporting evidence and trace entries in register
Check additions to allotment lists and cash records and agree totals to recorded movements
Ensure correct treatment of share premiums
Vouch issue expenses

Ensure it is clear which reserves are distributable

items: Check movements to minutes of Board’s meeting

Ensure disclosure of movements and related tax treatment

shortQuestions.question: List the points to be considered during verification of bank balances.

items: Agree the balances with the bankbook, and/or general ledger and bank statement.
Obtain reconciliation for the bank accounts in case of difference between bank book and bank statement.
Check that outstanding cheques have been cleared with the bank statement subsequent to the year-end.
Ask for any special reason if cheques have not been cleared subsequently.

shortQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the letter of confirmation from the bank?

answerBlocks.text: The purpose of the letter of confirmation from the bank is to confirm the bank balances and other matters by the bank directly to the auditor.
The letter is written by the auditors to the bank requesting confirmation of bank balances and allied matters directly to them.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the information requested from the bank in the standard letter of request for bank report.

items: Full title of account and balances thereon.
Accounts closed during the period.
Interest charged during the period.
Details of security and charges.
Details of investments or documents held.

shortQuestions.question: What details should be provided about bank accounts in the confirmation letter?

items: Full titles of all accounts together with the account numbers and balances thereon, including NIL.
Where the customer's name is the sole name in the title.
Where the customer's name is joined with other parties.
Where the account is in a trade name.
Information on any restrictions on the amounts (e.g. garnishee order, exchange control).

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain what information about security should be requested from the bank.

items: Details of any security formally charged to the bank, including the date and type of charge (e.g. pledge, hypothecation).
Particulars of any undertaking to assign assets to the bank.
Indicate if security is limited to any borrowing or if there is a prior, equal or subordinate charge.
Investments, bills of exchange, documents of title or other assets held but not charged.

shortQuestions.question: List the types of contingent liabilities to be confirmed by the bank.

items: Total of bills discounted for the customer, with recourse.
Details of any guarantees, bonds or indemnities given to the bank by the customer in favor of third parties.
Details of any guarantees, bonds or indemnities given by the bank on the customer's behalf, stating recourse details.
Total of acceptances.
Total of forward exchange contracts.
Total of outstanding liabilities under documentary credits.
Other contingent liabilities with details.

shortQuestions.question: What should the bank state if there is nothing to report against any item in the confirmation letter?

answerBlocks.text: The bank should state 'NONE' if there is nothing to report against any item.

shortQuestions.question: Define the positive and negative methods of obtaining debtor confirmation.

answerBlocks.text: **Positive Method:** The company requests the debtor to confirm his indebtedness to the company directly to the auditor and if there is disagreement, to state the balance as per his records with full particulars of the difference.

**Negative Method:** The company requests the debtor to communicate with the auditor only if he disagrees with the balance. If no communication is received within a specified time, the auditor may assume the balance is agreed.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between positive and negative confirmation in debtor verification.

rows: Confirm balance direct to auditor whether agreed or not.

When internal control system is not satisfactory or for significant balances.
When internal control is satisfactory or for large number of small balances.

shortQuestions.question: What procedures should an auditor follow if no reply is received to a positive confirmation request?

shortQuestions.question: What information does confirmation from debtors provide to the auditor?

Detection of irregularities such as teeming and lading, overdue balances, and incorrect balances.

shortQuestions.question: What does the auditor form an opinion on based on debtor confirmation information?

items: Reliability of debtor balances.
Quantum and nature of disputes existing between the company and its customers.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the audit procedures to verify Director’s Fee.

shortQuestions.question: What are the key audit checks related to Depreciation on Fixed Assets?

shortQuestions.question: What should an auditor check regarding the segregation of inventories during stock verification?

shortQuestions.question: Define audit sampling.

answerBlocks.text: Audit sampling means application of audit procedures to less than 100% of items appearing in an account balance or class of transactions to enable the auditor to form conclusion concerning that population.

shortQuestions.question: List the reasons why audit sampling is used.

items: Economic: Audit becomes cost effective.
Time: Complete check would take so long time.
Practical: Users do not expect 100% accuracy; materiality is important.
Psychological: A complete check would be boring for the audit staff.
Fruitfulness: A complete check would not add much to the worth of figures if few errors were discovered.

shortQuestions.question: Outline exceptions to audit sampling where a 100% check is necessary.

items: Categories which are few in number but of great importance (e.g., land and buildings).
Categories with special importance where materiality does not apply (e.g., directors' emoluments and loans).
Unusual, one-off, or exceptional items (e.g., accidental loss).
Any area where the auditor is put upon enquiry (e.g., legal matters, lawsuits).
High risk areas.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between statistical and judgmental sampling in auditing.

answerBlocks.text: Statistical sampling uses mathematical techniques to select and evaluate samples, while judgmental sampling relies on the auditor's experience and judgment to select sample size and items.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the objective of audit sampling.

answerBlocks.text: The objective of audit sampling is to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to determine with reasonable assurance whether the financial statements are free of material misstatements.

shortQuestions.question: What is meant by 'population' and 'sampling units' in audit sampling?

answerBlocks.text: Population means the set of data, such as account balances or transactions, while sampling units are the individual items making up the population.

shortQuestions.question: Define audit materiality (tolerable error) and its significance in audit sampling.

answerBlocks.text: Tolerable error is the maximum error magnitude that can exist without damaging the true and fair view of financial statements. It guides the auditor in planning tests to ensure actual errors are less than this threshold.

shortQuestions.question: List and briefly describe the components of audit risk.

items: Inherent risk: Risk attached to a population due to factors like industry type or history of errors.
Control risk: Risk that internal controls will not detect or prevent material errors.
Detection risk: Risk that auditor's procedures will not detect material errors.

shortQuestions.question: Outline factors an auditor should consider when deciding whether to use sampling.

items: Materiality of the population.
Number of items in the population.
Reliability of other evidence.
Cost and time considerations.
Combination of evidence seeking methods.

shortQuestions.question: List the stages of audit sampling.

items: Planning the sample.
Selection of the items to be tested.
Testing the items.
Evaluating the results.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the meaning of judgmental sampling and mention its advantages.

answerBlocks.text: Judgmental sampling means selecting a sample size based on the auditor's judgment of what is desirable.

items: Well understood and refined by experience.
Allows auditor's judgment and expertise to be applied.
No special knowledge of statistics required.
Audit time is spent on auditing rather than mathematics.

shortQuestions.question: List disadvantages of judgmental sampling.

items: Unscientific approach.
Usually results in sample sizes that are too large.
No quantitative results obtained.
Personal bias in sample selection.
No real logic to sample size or selection.
Sample selection can be imbalanced to auditor's needs.
Conclusions are often vague or uncertain.

shortQuestions.question: Define statistical sampling in auditing.

answerBlocks.text: Statistical sampling in auditing is the process of drawing inferences about a large volume of data by examining a sample, using principles from the discipline of statistics.

shortQuestions.question: List the advantages of using statistical sampling in auditing.

items: It is scientific.
It is defensible / justifiable.
It provides precise mathematical statements about probabilities of being correct.
It is efficient - overlarge sample sizes are not taken.
It tends to cause uniform standards among different audit firms.
It can be used by lower grade staff who may not be able to apply judgment needed by judgmental sampling.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the disadvantages of statistical sampling mentioned in the lesson.

items: It is not always fully understood, so false conclusions may be drawn.
Time may be spent on mathematics that might be better spent on auditing.
Audit judgment takes second place to precise mathematics.
Often several attributes of transactions or documents are tested at the same time, which statistics does not easily incorporate.
It is inflexible.

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain the characteristics an audit sample should have.

items: Random: Each item has an equal or specified chance of selection.
Representative: Contains similar proportions of differing items as the population.
Protective: Focuses more intensive auditing on high value or high risk items.
Unpredictable: Client cannot know or guess which items will be examined.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between haphazard sampling and simple random sampling.

answerBlocks.text: Haphazard sampling involves choosing items subjectively but avoiding bias, and is acceptable for non-statistical sampling but insufficiently accurate for statistical sampling.
Simple random sampling assigns numbers to all items and selects numbers so that every item has an equal chance of selection, typically using random number tables or computer-generated numbers.

shortQuestions.question: List and briefly describe three sample selection methods used in auditing.

items: Stratified Sampling: Dividing the population into sub-populations (strata) and sampling each, often checking high value items 100%.
Cluster Sampling: Selecting a random cluster (group) and examining all items in it; may not be representative.
Random Systematic Sampling: Making a random start and selecting every nth item thereafter; saves work but may not be representative.

shortQuestions.question: What is value weighted selection (Monetary Unit Sampling) and why is it popular in auditing?

answerBlocks.text: Value weighted selection uses the currency unit value rather than items as the sampling population. It is popular because it is appropriate for large variance populations, suited where errors are not expected, and implicitly considers the auditor’s concept of materiality.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the procedure of monetary unit sampling with respect to sample size and selection.

items: Determine sample size based on population size, minimum unacceptable error rate (materiality), and desired Beta risk.
List items in the population with their balances and cumulative totals.
Take a random start and select every nth currency unit thereafter (systematic sampling).
If a particular currency unit is selected, the whole balance containing that unit is examined and any error quantified.
Evaluate results to conclude confidence level and whether further investigation or larger samples are needed.

shortQuestions.question: Why is monetary unit sampling especially useful for testing overstatement and not suitable for testing creditors?

answerBlocks.text: Monetary unit sampling is useful for testing overstatement where significant understatements are not expected, such as debtors, fixed assets, and stocks. It is not suitable for creditors where understatement is the primary characteristic to be tested.

shortQuestions.question: What does it mean for an audit sample to be 'protective' and why is this important?

answerBlocks.text: A protective sample means that the auditor focuses more intensive auditing on high value or high risk items. This is important to safeguard the auditor by ensuring that items with greater potential impact are examined more thoroughly.

lessons.title: CONSIDERING THE WORK OF INTERNAL AUDITING

shortQuestions.question: Define internal auditing.

answerBlocks.text: Internal auditing means an appraisal activity established within an entity as a service to the entity. Its functions include examining, evaluating and monitoring the adequacy and effectiveness of the accounting and internal control system.

shortQuestions.question: List the main objectives of the internal audit function.

items: Review and assessment of the internal control procedures and accounting system.
Examination of financial and operating information for management, including detailed testing of transactions and balances.
Review of efficiency, economy and effectiveness of operation.
Review of compliance with laws, regulations, management policy and other internal requirements.

shortQuestions.question: Distinguish between internal and external auditors in terms of responsibility and scope of work.

rows: Determined by statute or mutual agreement
Ensure accounting system and controls operate efficiently

shortQuestions.question: Briefly explain why external auditors need to understand internal auditing activities.

answerBlocks.text: External auditors should obtain a sufficient understanding of internal audit activities to assist in planning the audit and developing an effective audit approach. Effective internal auditing may allow a reduction in the procedures performed by external auditors but cannot eliminate them entirely.

shortQuestions.question: Outline the criteria an external auditor should consider when assessing the internal audit function.

items: Organizational status: Evaluate the internal auditor's freedom in performing duties and communication with external auditor.
Scope and objectives of internal audit function: Examine assignments and management's response to recommendations.
Technical competence: Ascertain adequacy of training and proficiency of internal audit staff.
Due professional care: Consider if work is properly planned, supervised, reviewed and documented.

shortQuestions.question: List the common means adopted by both internal and external auditors to achieve their objectives.

answerBlocks.text: One common means adopted by both internal and external auditors is the evaluation of internal control.

shortQuestions.question: Explain the importance of liaison and coordination between internal and external auditors.

items: Initial planning to formulate a joint approach to minimize duplicated tests.
Regular meetings during the year to discuss audit matters.
Exchange of knowledge about significant matters affecting each other's work.

shortQuestions.question: What steps should an external auditor take when relying on the work of the internal auditor?

items: Review internal audit working papers to ensure audit programs are adequate.
Verify work is performed by trained staff and properly supervised and reviewed.
Confirm sufficient appropriate audit evidence was obtained.
Assess if conclusions and reports are appropriate and based on work done.
Ensure exceptions or unusual items have been properly resolved.
Record all working papers received from internal audit.
Test the work of the internal auditor.

shortQuestions.question: Outline methods an external auditor can use to test the work of internal auditing.

items: Re-performing the work done by internal auditor on a test basis to ensure consistent results.
Selecting a few similar items and performing independent tests.
Observation of internal auditing procedures.

shortQuestions.question: Why can internal auditors not enjoy the same degree of independence as external auditors?

answerBlocks.text: Internal auditors are employees of the entity and therefore cannot be independent. In contrast, external auditors are required to be independent of the enterprise and have statutory responsibility for reporting on financial statements.
